abstract: Learning and stress resilience can be influenced by recent experiences. Research has traditionally focused on the effects of negative situations and stressors on subsequent learning and stress resilience, while knowledge is limited regarding the effects of positive experiences. We aimed to examine the impact of a pre-session brief positive experience on dogs' learning and stress resilience. Pet dogs were quasi-randomly assigned to the experimental (n = 20) or control (n = 20) group, counterbalanced for age, sex, and breed clade. Experimental dogs received a session intended to provide a positive experience, which included a 15 min walk on a long leash, human interaction, exploration, playing, and olfactory-based foraging. Control dogs were kept on leash in an office without being allowed to explore nor interact with their owner or the experimenters for 15 min. After 60 s of habituation to the testing room, all dogs were taught to nose-touch the experimenter's hand. After the Learning phase, there was a 2 min Disruption phase, in which a remote-controlled car moved inside of a tub at a distance. Measures included the number of hand touches in each phase, the latency to return to the task, and general stress and affiliative behaviours. No differences were observed in the Learning phase. Surprisingly, experimental dogs exhibited higher stress levels than control dogs during the Disruption phase. These dogs also spent a significantly higher proportion of time in proximity to their owners, which could be interpreted as reassurance-seeking behaviour. Contrary to our predictions, exposure to a brief positive experience did not impact learning and, surprisingly, seemed to have made dogs more susceptible to stress during the Disruption phase. Several possible explanations are discussed, including the possibility of an unintentional induction of a negative emotional state by the termination of the positive experience, as well as differences in arousal, or habituation to the indoor environment.

mcqs.q: What effect did the brief pre-session positive experience have on dogs' learning phase performance?
mcqs.e: No differences were observed in the Learning phase between experimental and control dogs.

mcqs.q: During the Disruption phase, experimental (positive-experience) dogs showed what compared to controls?
mcqs.e: Unexpectedly, experimental dogs showed higher stress and more owner-proximity (reassurance-seeking).

mcqs.q: Which explanation did the authors propose for the surprising stress finding?
o: Abruptly ending the positive experience may have induced a negative emotional state
The learning task was too easy
mcqs.e: Terminating the positive experience may have unintentionally induced a negative emotional state.

title: Variation in food-maximizing behaviour as a function of context, breed, and individual characteristics: A study of Labrador Retrievers and German Shepherd Dogs
citation: Amin Azadian, Alexandra Protopopova. Variation in food-maximizing behaviour as a function of context, breed, and individual characteristics: A study of Labrador Retrievers and German Shepherd Dogs. Behavioural Processes. 2026.
abstract: Food motivation is widely recognized as a fundamental factor shaping domestic dog behaviour. However, it remains unclear whether different behavioural experimental paradigms capture distinct motivational components, and whether factors known to shape dogs' food motivation differentially contribute to performance across these measures. We assessed Labrador Retrievers (n = 24) and German Shepherd Dogs (n = 24), breeds that are commonly characterized as highly food and toy responsive, respectively, across two food-maximizing behavioural paradigms: a progressive ratio (PR) task measuring effort expenditure and an uncertainty-based probabilistic choice task quantifying win-stay and lose-shift (WSLS) strategies. Using mixed-effects models, we found that Labradors reached significantly higher PR breakpoints than German Shepherd Dogs, with this difference persisting regardless of training level. Furthermore, age had a breed-dependent effect on PR performance, such that increasing age was associated with lower PR breakpoints particularly in Labradors. In the WSLS task, breed differences emerged only through interactions with questionnaire-based measures of food motivation: higher scores predicted increased win-stay and reduced lose-shift tendencies specifically in Labradors, consistent with sustained motivation to persist with a previously chosen option despite occasional nonreward. Behavioural characteristics also shaped outcome-dependent strategies, as higher owner-rated frustration was linked to increased switching tendency, particularly after rewarded trials. Together, these results demonstrate that different behavioural measures likely capture distinct dimensions of food motivation and predictors of food-maximizing behavioural tendencies are breed-dependent. A multi-measure approach is therefore essential for comprehensively evaluating how motivation translates into behaviour across diverse food-related contexts.

mcqs.q: Which breed reached significantly higher progressive-ratio breakpoints (worked harder for food)?
mcqs.e: Labradors reached higher PR breakpoints than German Shepherds, regardless of training level.

mcqs.q: Were the predictors of food-maximizing behaviour breed-dependent?
mcqs.e: Predictors of food-maximizing behaviour differed by breed (e.g., food-motivation effects specific to Labradors).

mcqs.q: What approach do the authors recommend for evaluating food motivation?
mcqs.e: Different tasks capture distinct dimensions, so a multi-measure approach is essential.

title: Changes in cognitive performance following repeated exposure to a hand-touch learning task across breed clades of domestic dogs (Canis familiaris)
citation: Amin Azadian, Alexandra Protopopova. Changes in cognitive performance following repeated exposure to a hand-touch learning task across breed clades of domestic dogs (Canis familiaris). Animal Cognition. 2026.
abstract: Selective breeding for specialized functional roles has resulted in consistent differences among domestic dog breeds in a range of cognitive capacities, as demonstrated by standardized cognitive assessments. What remains uncertain is whether these breed differences extend beyond initial task performance to influence how dogs adjust their behaviour or improve their performance when they are re-tested on the same tasks. In the present study, we used a structured hand-touch learning task to examine changes in Discrimination, Reversal learning, and resistance to Extinction performances across two testing sessions in 105 dogs representing five breed clades. Statistical analyses accounted for demographic variables, reward responsiveness, impulsivity, and training history. Dogs showed limited changes in learning performance across sessions, with statistically significant improvement observed only in Reversal learning from Test 1 to Test 2. Most breed-clade differences in average performance found during the initial test were no longer evident at Test 2. There was also limited evidence that breed clades differed in the extent of their performance change over time. Taken together, these results suggest that initial performance differences across breed clades likely reflect breed-specific cognitive profiles that shape how dogs engage with novel learning tasks. Following re-exposure to the task, average performance tends to improve and potentially mask the initial between-clade differences, although the magnitude of improvement appears broadly similar across breed clades. These findings highlight the importance of considering both initial performance and prior experience when interpreting breed differences in learning and cognitive capacities.

mcqs.q: What happened to most breed-clade performance differences upon re-testing?
mcqs.e: Most initial between-clade differences were no longer evident at Test 2 as performance improved.

mcqs.q: Which performance showed statistically significant improvement from Test 1 to Test 2?
mcqs.e: Only reversal learning improved significantly between sessions.

mcqs.q: What do the findings imply for interpreting breed differences in cognition?
o: Both initial performance and prior experience must be considered
A single test is always definitive
mcqs.e: Re-exposure can mask initial differences, so prior experience must be accounted for.

title: The Association of Shelter Veterinarians' Guidelines for Humane Rabbit Housing in Animal Shelters
authors: Erica Schumacher, Elizabeth Berliner, Sarah Hicks, Chumkee Aziz, Emilia Wong Gordon, Zarah Hedge, Kate Hurley, Jessica Reed, Rebecca Stuntebeck
journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health
citation: Erica Schumacher, Elizabeth Berliner, Sarah Hicks, Chumkee Aziz, Emilia Wong Gordon, Zarah Hedge, Kate Hurley, Jessica Reed, Rebecca Stuntebeck. The Association of Shelter Veterinarians' Guidelines for Humane Rabbit Housing in Animal Shelters. Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health. 2025.
abstract: Purpose: "The purpose of this document is to provide guidelines for the humane housing of rabbits in animal shelters, rescue groups, and foster homes, based on expert input and available scientific research." About this document: "This project began as a discussion of shelter medicine experts exploring the needs of rabbits in animal shelters and recognizing the lack of resources specific to this unique species." The document focuses specifically on rabbit housing (with intake and husbandry topics addressed only as they relate to housing), was developed by shelter medicine veterinarians through a comprehensive literature review and group consensus, and prioritizes published references on rabbit housing and behavior wherever feasible. It establishes minimum space and environmental standards (enabling natural behaviors, hiding/enrichment, appropriate light cycles for crepuscular rabbits, and flooring that reduces pododermatitis), and includes an appendix on Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease Virus 2 (RHDV2) mitigation, biosecurity, and vaccination, framed within a Capacity for Care approach.

mcqs.q: According to the Association of Shelter Veterinarians (ASV) guidelines for humane rabbit housing in animal shelters, how are rabbits characterised in terms of their activity pattern and role as prey animals, relevant to designing appropriate light cycles and environmental requirements?
mcqs.e: Rabbits are crepuscular prey animals, which informs the housing requirements: appropriate light cycles, hiding spots, and enrichment are recommended by the ASV guidelines to support their natural behavioural needs and reduce stress.

mcqs.q: What flooring is recommended to reduce pododermatitis in sheltered rabbits?
mcqs.e: Non-wire flooring is specified to reduce pododermatitis.

mcqs.q: Which viral disease is highlighted in the appendix as a key shelter biosecurity threat for rabbits?
mcqs.e: The appendix addresses RHDV2 mitigation, biosecurity, and vaccination.

title: Short-term storage conditions do not affect canine fecal cortisol and secretory immunoglobulin A concentrations
authors: Lenz OC, Powell L, Reinhard CL, Watson B
citation: Lenz OC, Powell L, Reinhard CL, Watson B. Short-term storage conditions do not affect canine fecal cortisol and secretory immunoglobulin A concentrations. Scientific Reports. 2026.
abstract: Fecal cortisol and secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) are frequently used biomarkers in animal welfare, wildlife conservation, and other fields. However, these research settings often lack immediate access to a -80 degrees C freezer or other ultra-low temperature storage equipment. This study aims to determine whether canine fecal cortisol and sIgA concentrations remain stable over 24 h at either ambient temperature or on wet ice. Fecal samples were collected from 10 adult dogs housed in two Philadelphia area animal shelters in May and June of 2024. After aliquoting, baseline samples were frozen on dry ice within 15 minutes of defecation. Remaining aliquots were stored at ambient temperature (15-21 degrees C) or on wet ice (4 degrees C) for 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, or 24 hours before freezing on dry ice. Cortisol and sIgA concentrations were quantified using ELISAs and analyzed with a linear mixed effects model. No significant differences were found between time points or storage conditions. These data show that concentrations of fecal canine cortisol and sIgA remain stable if stored unfrozen for 24 hours. Immediate freezing at -80 degrees C does not appear to be necessary for accurate quantification of these analytes. This knowledge removes logistical and regulatory barriers to conducting quality noninvasive research in animal shelter, clinical, and field settings.

mcqs.q: A study collected canine fecal samples from shelter dogs and stored them at ambient temperature (15–21°C (59–69.8°F)) or on wet ice (4°C (39.2°F)) for up to 24 hours before freezing. Cortisol and secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) concentrations were then measured. What were the findings?
o: Stable with no significant differences across time points or conditions
mcqs.e: No significant differences were found across time points or storage conditions over 24 hours, demonstrating that canine fecal cortisol and sIgA remain stable when stored unfrozen at ambient temperature or on wet ice.

mcqs.q: A study examined whether canine fecal cortisol and secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) concentrations remain stable when stored at ambient temperature or on wet ice for up to 24 hours. Is immediate freezing at −80°C (−112°F) necessary for accurate quantification of these biomarkers?
o: No, it does not appear necessary
mcqs.e: Fecal cortisol and sIgA concentrations remained stable unfrozen for 24 hours under both storage conditions, so immediate ultra-low-temperature freezing is not required for accurate measurement.

mcqs.q: What practical benefit do the authors highlight?
o: Removal of cold-storage barriers to noninvasive shelter/field research
Requirement for ultra-low freezers on site
mcqs.e: The stability removes logistical/regulatory barriers to noninvasive welfare research without specialized cold storage.

title: Shelter medicine rotations help students rethink care for underserved communities: a qualitative analysis of veterinary student reflective journals
authors: Jafarian S, Powell L, Reinhard CL, Watson B
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
citation: Jafarian S, Powell L, Reinhard CL, Watson B. Shelter medicine rotations help students rethink care for underserved communities: a qualitative analysis of veterinary student reflective journals. Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association. 2026.
abstract: The researchers examined how shelter medicine rotations influence veterinary student perspectives. They analyzed reflective journals from 53 students at the University of Pennsylvania's School of Veterinary Medicine between January 2015 and July 2019 using qualitative content analysis. Eight major themes emerged, including student perspectives of owners, pets, neighborhoods, community outreach, and self; the learning process; the role of pets as social catalysts; and trust. Students demonstrated meaningful shifts in how they viewed pet owners. The study found that community engagement, both in duration and variety, helped students develop critical interpersonal abilities including social competence, cultural humility, and contextualized decision-making. The authors conclude that structured, reflective community-based learning can enhance emotional intelligence and prepare students for serving diverse populations. They advocate for integrating sustained, diverse, and ethically grounded community engagement into veterinary curricula. (J Am Vet Med Assoc 2026; 264(4):476-484.)

mcqs.q: What meaningful shift did students show after shelter medicine rotations?
o: Shifts in how they viewed pet owners
mcqs.e: Students demonstrated meaningful shifts in how they viewed pet owners in underserved communities.

mcqs.q: Which competencies did community engagement help students develop?
mcqs.e: Engagement built social competence, cultural humility, and contextualized decision-making.

mcqs.q: A 2026 qualitative analysis of reflective journals from 53 veterinary students completing shelter medicine rotations at the University of Pennsylvania found that community engagement enhanced social competence, cultural humility, and emotional intelligence. What do the authors of that study advocate for veterinary curricula?
o: Integrating sustained, diverse, ethically grounded community engagement
Limiting rotations to a single day

title: Insights into shelter dog outcomes using behavioral and biological stress markers
authors: Powell L, Graham K, Grant L, Lenz O, Reinhard CL, Yost H, Anderson E, Watson B
citation: Powell L, Graham K, Grant L, Lenz O, Reinhard CL, Yost H, Anderson E, Watson B. Insights into shelter dog outcomes using behavioral and biological stress markers. Physiology & Behavior. 2025.
abstract: The research team investigated whether behavioral observations and stress biomarkers could help predict outcomes for shelter dogs. Over nine months, they studied 224 dogs from three Pennsylvania shelters, collecting fecal samples and recording behavioral videos at two timepoints (within 48 hours and 7-9 days after entry). Key findings indicated that at shelter entry, behavior patterns differed significantly by outcome. Dogs returned to owners demonstrated increased panting while those euthanized or transferred showed less time sitting than adopted dogs. After one week, human-directed behaviors became predictive; dogs that were adopted or transferred spent more time standing with their front paws on the cage and wagging tails compared to euthanized animals. Cortisol levels were higher in adopted versus transferred dogs at baseline but showed no significant difference by week one. Immunoglobulin A levels did not meaningfully correlate with outcomes. The authors concluded that in-kennel behavioral observations may provide the most useful information for shelters to assess stress, while biological markers warranted further investigation into how dogs adapt to shelter environments.

mcqs.q: In a 9-month study of 224 shelter dogs from three Pennsylvania shelters that collected fecal samples and behavioral videos at two timepoints to compare behavioral and biological stress markers by outcome group, which measure did the researchers conclude was most useful for shelters to assess stress?
mcqs.e: In-kennel behavioral observations may provide the most useful stress information for shelters, while biological markers warranted further investigation.

mcqs.q: How did immunoglobulin A (IgA) levels relate to dog outcomes?
o: Did not meaningfully correlate with outcomes
mcqs.e: IgA levels did not meaningfully correlate with outcomes.

mcqs.q: After one week, which behaviors predicted adoption/transfer over euthanasia?
o: Human-directed behaviors such as front paws on cage and tail wagging
mcqs.e: At one week, human-directed behaviors (front paws on cage, tail wagging) predicted adoption/transfer.

title: Confirmation of Efficacy of Commonly Used Veterinary Surface Disinfectants Against Carbapenemase-Producing Enterobacterales Isolated from Pets
authors: Garcia LC, Dietrich J, Watson B, Reinhard CL, Cole SD
journal: Journal of the American Animal Hospital Association
citation: Garcia LC, Dietrich J, Watson B, Reinhard CL, Cole SD. Confirmation of Efficacy of Commonly Used Veterinary Surface Disinfectants Against Carbapenemase-Producing Enterobacterales Isolated from Pets. Journal of the American Animal Hospital Association. 2025.
abstract: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) are an emerging public health threat in both human and veterinary medicine. As antibiotic resistance grows, there is increased importance in preventing the spread and transmission of these organisms by using appropriate infection prevention and biosecurity measures. The goal of this study was to test the efficacy of commonly used disinfectants in the veterinary setting against CPE strains. A total of 10 bacterial strains (9 CPE and 1 control strain) and 5 disinfectants were evaluated. Effective disinfection (at least a 3-log kill) was found at the manufacturer's contact time for all strains when paired with all products except for one strain (47422-21) of Enterobacter hormaechei, which only had a 2-log for the accelerated hydrogen peroxide product and a 1-log reduction for the quaternary ammonium compound product. When used according to manufacturer recommendations, the five surface disinfectants tested were effective in vitro against the majority of CPE of animal origin that were evaluated. (J Am Anim Hosp Assoc 2025; 61(4):83-89; DOI 10.5326/JAAHA-MS-7440.)

mcqs.q: In a study testing five veterinary surface disinfectants against Carbapenemase-Producing Enterobacterales (CPE) strains isolated from pets, at the manufacturer's recommended contact time, most disinfectant–strain combinations achieved at least what log reduction?
mcqs.e: Effective disinfection (at least a 3-log kill) was achieved at the manufacturer's contact time for the great majority of CPE strains tested.

mcqs.q: Which organism strain resisted the accelerated hydrogen peroxide and quaternary ammonium products?
mcqs.e: One Enterobacter hormaechei strain showed only 2-log and 1-log reductions for those products.

mcqs.q: What is the key biosecurity takeaway?
o: Correct contact time and product selection are critical for effective disinfection
mcqs.e: Products worked when used per label, underscoring correct contact time and product choice.

title: Public perceptions of free-roaming dogs and cats in India and the United States
authors: Sensharma R, Reinhard CL, Powell L, Watson B
journal: Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science
citation: Sensharma R, Reinhard CL, Powell L, Watson B. Public perceptions of free-roaming dogs and cats in India and the United States. Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science. 2025.
abstract: This cross-sectional investigation examined differences in how Indian and American communities perceive free-roaming canines and felines. Survey data from 498 respondents (210 Indian, 288 American) collected between August 2021 and February 2022 revealed that Indian participants largely viewed these animals as community members, with significantly greater support for allowing them to roam freely. Both groups expressed welfare concerns, though Americans were more likely to cite welfare, public health, and wildlife risks. American respondents favored adoption and euthanasia strategies, while Indian respondents preferred spay/neuter, vaccinate and release strategies for population management. The findings emphasize tailoring interventions to reflect local cultural values regarding free-roaming animal populations. (J Appl Anim Welf Sci 2025; 28(4):563-577; DOI 10.1080/10888705.2024.2374078.)

mcqs.q: How did Indian respondents predominantly view free-roaming dogs and cats?
mcqs.e: Indian participants largely viewed free-roaming animals as community members and supported free roaming.

mcqs.q: Which management strategy did Indian respondents prefer?
mcqs.e: Indian respondents favored spay/neuter, vaccinate and release; Americans favored adoption and euthanasia.

mcqs.q: A cross-sectional survey comparing Indian (n=210) and American (n=288) public perceptions of free-roaming dogs and cats found substantial cultural differences in preferred management strategies. What is the study's central recommendation for designing population management interventions?
o: Apply a single identical global policy
Tailor interventions to local cultural values
mcqs.e: Because communities differ markedly in how they view free-roaming animals, interventions should be tailored to reflect local cultural values.

title: Toxoplasmal meningoencephalitis in a 14 week-old shelter cat with presumed feline infectious peritonitis
authors: Amira Abdu, M Erin Henry, Nicole M André, Andrew D Miller, Manigandan Lejeune, Elizabeth A Berliner, Gary R Whittaker
journal: Veterinary Parasitology: Regional Studies and Reports
citation: Amira Abdu, M Erin Henry, Nicole M André, Andrew D Miller, Manigandan Lejeune, Elizabeth A Berliner, Gary R Whittaker. Toxoplasmal meningoencephalitis in a 14 week-old shelter cat with presumed feline infectious peritonitis. Veterinary Parasitology: Regional Studies and Reports. 2025.
abstract: Toxoplasmal meningoencephalitis is a sporadic condition that is often misdiagnosed antemortem, frequently resulting in euthanasia especially in resource-limited settings. Here we report a case of a 7-week-old female domestic shorthair cat from an animal shelter who presented in a compromised condition and continued to display clinical signs consistent with a 'failure to thrive' kitten. Weight loss and decreased activity were observed, and later on, neurological dysfunction became apparent. Based on clinical signs, non-effusive feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) was strongly suspected. Other possible conditions, such as a portosystemic shunt or toxoplasmosis, were also considered. Due to a poor prognosis, euthanasia was elected. Molecular testing at necropsy revealed no evidence for feline coronavirus infection; however, histopathological examination of the brain tissue revealed disseminated necrotizing meningoencephalitis with the presence of Toxoplasma gondii bradyzoites and tachyzoites, which was further confirmed by PCR and sequence analysis. In hindsight, it became clear that the kitten's failure to thrive was due to severe neurological compromise caused by overwhelming toxoplasmosis infection. This report underscores the diagnostic challenges associated with feline neurological disorders.

mcqs.q: A failure-to-thrive shelter kitten with progressive neurologic signs was clinically suspected to have non-effusive FIP. What ultimately established the true diagnosis?
o: Necropsy histopathology with Toxoplasma PCR confirmation
mcqs.e: Diagnosis required postmortem brain histopathology showing Toxoplasma bradyzoites/tachyzoites, confirmed by PCR.

mcqs.q: A shelter kitten presented with failure to thrive and progressive neurological signs, was clinically suspected to have non-effusive feline infectious peritonitis (FIP), and was euthanized due to poor prognosis. At necropsy, what did molecular testing for feline coronavirus reveal?
o: Necropsy molecular testing found no feline coronavirus
Serology was strongly positive for coronavirus
mcqs.e: No feline coronavirus was detected; histopathology instead revealed Toxoplasma gondii bradyzoites and tachyzoites in brain tissue, confirmed by PCR — showing overwhelming toxoplasmosis rather than FIP.

mcqs.q: For neurologic signs in a failure-to-thrive shelter kitten, which should remain on the differential alongside FIP?
mcqs.e: The authors stress keeping toxoplasmosis and portosystemic shunt in mind, noting antemortem diagnosis is limited in resource-poor shelters.

title: Don't Forget Fido: A Call to Include Pets in Public Health Research and Policy to Support Families and Communities
authors: Emily D Dolan, Brett Wyker, Elizabeth A Berliner, Matt Goldweber, Ana Hernandez
citation: Emily D Dolan, Brett Wyker, Elizabeth A Berliner, Matt Goldweber, Ana Hernandez. Don't Forget Fido: A Call to Include Pets in Public Health Research and Policy to Support Families and Communities. American Journal of Public Health. 2025.
abstract: No structured abstract is published; this is an editorial/commentary in the American Journal of Public Health (2025) authored by members of the ASPCA's Strategy and Research, Shelter Medicine Services, and Community Engagement teams — a One Health call to action. The ASPCA estimates ~6.3 million pets enter US shelters yearly and almost 1 million are euthanised. Involuntary family–pet separation creates stress, grief and safety risk for families, is dangerous for pets, and overwhelms the animal-welfare social system. Three major challenges for families and pets: (1) a severe shortage of pet-inclusive rental housing; (2) family vulnerability during natural disasters; and (3) increasing lack of access to veterinary care. The authors argue we must align animal welfare and public health into a strong alliance so that research and policy effectively include pets — animal-welfare and veterinary professionals must be integrated into public-health research and policy discussions at every level.

mcqs.q: A 2025 editorial in the American Journal of Public Health by ASPCA researchers, titled 'Don't Forget Fido,' argues from a One Health perspective that companion animals are integral to the wellbeing of families and communities. What is the central argument of this commentary?
o: Pets should be excluded from public health data to reduce confounding
Pets should be explicitly included in public health research and policy
Public health should focus only on humans
mcqs.e: The piece argues companion animals must be incorporated into public health research, data, and policy because they are integral to family and community wellbeing.

mcqs.q: According to the 2025 One Health editorial 'Don't Forget Fido' in the American Journal of Public Health (authored by ASPCA researchers), which argues that companion animals are integral to family and community wellbeing, excluding pets from public health support services creates:
o: Gaps in support services for families and communities
mcqs.e: Leaving pets out of support systems creates gaps because pets are integral to the wellbeing of families and communities.

mcqs.q: The 2025 publication 'Don't Forget Fido' in the American Journal of Public Health (authored by ASPCA researchers), which calls for including pets in public health research and policy, is best described as:
o: An editorial / One Health call to action
mcqs.e: It is an editorial/commentary framed as a One Health call to action with no structured abstract, authored by ASPCA researchers.

title: Recognizing Non-Human Animals as a Vulnerable Class in Assessments of "Dangerousness to Others": Application in Animal Hoarding
citation: Gary J. Patronek, Martha Smith-Blackmore. Recognizing Non-Human Animals as a Vulnerable Class in Assessments of "Dangerousness to Others": Application in Animal Hoarding. Behavioral Sciences & the Law. 2026.
abstract: We argue that the forensic concept of "dangerousness" should be expanded to protect non-human animals when danger is readily foreseeable and before it materializes into substantial harm. The criminal justice approach is limited in this respect because it relies on cruelty statutes that are largely reactive, embodying the adage that "some must suffer first" before intervention can occur. We demonstrate that dangerousness principles and/or language are already embedded-often implicitly and sometimes explicitly-in at least five areas of animal law. We highlight the well-accepted "grave disability" criteria used in assessing dangerousness to self because of the parallels to the deficits noted in animal hoarding, with the main difference being the absence or presence of animals. A civil approach focused on forfeiture (and when appropriate, mental health intervention) rather than prosecution could help bridge the gap between the care animals deserve and the deficiencies that criminal law will currently tolerate.

mcqs.q: In a 2026 legal analysis arguing that the forensic concept of 'dangerousness' should be expanded to protect non-human animals before harm materializes, why do the authors consider criminal cruelty statutes limited for protecting hoarded animals?
o: They are reactive, requiring harm before intervention
They are purely civil in nature
mcqs.e: Cruelty statutes embody the adage that 'some must suffer first' — they are largely reactive, so intervention lags behind foreseeable harm.

mcqs.q: A 2026 legal analysis of 'dangerousness' principles applied to animal hoarding critiques reactive criminal prosecution. What alternative approach do the authors propose for better protecting hoarded animals?
o: Doing nothing until substantial harm occurs
A civil forfeiture approach paired with mental health intervention
mcqs.e: They favor a civil/forfeiture route with mental health intervention over reactive criminal prosecution, to bridge the gap between the care animals deserve and what criminal law currently tolerates.

mcqs.q: In the 2026 article 'Recognizing Non-Human Animals as a Vulnerable Class in Assessments of Dangerousness to Others,' the deficits seen in animal hoarding are likened to which existing legal dangerousness criterion?
mcqs.e: The authors draw on the well-accepted 'grave disability' criteria used in assessing dangerousness to self, noting the main difference is the absence or presence of animals.

title: Design and Application of an Evaluation Tool to Assess World Organization for Animal Health Competencies for Graduating (Day One) Veterinarians
authors: Andrew E Hoet, S Swisher, S Tomasi, T Fentie, A Melaku, S Nigatu, A Mengistu, A Assefa, Jeanette O'Quin, Jason W Stull, Wondwossen Gebreyes, Christina T Hammons, Amanda Berrian
citation: Andrew E Hoet, S Swisher, S Tomasi, T Fentie, A Melaku, S Nigatu, A Mengistu, A Assefa, Jeanette O'Quin, Jason W Stull, Wondwossen Gebreyes, Christina T Hammons, Amanda Berrian. Design and Application of an Evaluation Tool to Assess World Organization for Animal Health Competencies for Graduating (Day One) Veterinarians. Journal of Veterinary Medical Education. 2025.
abstract: Graduating competent veterinarians with the appropriate knowledge and skills to support and strengthen their country's National Veterinary Services is a key priority for veterinary institutions globally. The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) developed a set of Day One Competencies that should be expected of every veterinary graduate. Veterinary schools need to be able to assess the coverage of these competencies in their curriculum and determine the level of proficiency of their graduates. This article describes the iterative design and development process used to create a semi-quantitative, competency-based assessment survey. The Evaluation Tool for WOAH Day One Graduating Veterinarian Competencies is used as part of a stepwise process to systematically assess a veterinary curriculum regarding these competencies. This tool was developed and tested at the University of Gondar College of Veterinary Medicine and Animal Sciences in Ethiopia. The Evaluation Tool was successful in systematically collecting, measuring, and analyzing the perceptions of faculty, senior veterinary students, recent graduates, and external stakeholders about the level of proficiency of graduates in all 19 WOAH Day One Competencies. It was specifically designed to be used in conjunction with curriculum mapping to provide a full picture of how effectively these competencies were taught and identify gaps that needed to be addressed. This tool, the supporting resources, and the methodology are now globally accessible to all veterinary institutions, enabling them to revise and update their curricula and, ultimately, improve the training of the future veterinary workforce to support veterinary services in their respective countries.

mcqs.q: A semi-quantitative evaluation tool was developed and tested at the University of Gondar, Ethiopia, to assess how well a veterinary curriculum covers the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) Day One Competencies expected of all graduating veterinarians. How many WOAH Day One Competencies does this tool assess?
mcqs.e: The tool systematically collects and measures perceptions of faculty, students, and graduates across all 19 WOAH Day One Competencies.

mcqs.q: A semi-quantitative evaluation tool for assessing World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) Day One Competencies in graduating veterinarians is specifically designed to be used alongside what, in order to provide a full picture of how effectively those competencies are being taught?
mcqs.e: The tool is designed to be used in conjunction with curriculum mapping to show how effectively competencies are taught and to identify gaps that need to be addressed.

mcqs.q: The semi-quantitative Evaluation Tool for World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) Day One Graduating Veterinarian Competencies, now made globally accessible to veterinary institutions, was originally developed and tested at which institution?
mcqs.e: The tool was developed and tested at the University of Gondar College of Veterinary Medicine and Animal Sciences in Ethiopia before being made globally accessible.

title: Using Distance Education to Teach the AAVMC's Spectrum of Care Subcompetencies: Positive Changes in Self-Efficacy as Self-Reported by Students Enrolled from Multiple Colleges of Veterinary Medicine in the United States
authors: Kristin Jankowski, J Claire Schuch, Kaitlyn V Andres, Julie K Levy, Terry G Spencer
citation: Kristin Jankowski, J Claire Schuch, Kaitlyn V Andres, Julie K Levy, Terry G Spencer. Using Distance Education to Teach the AAVMC's Spectrum of Care Subcompetencies: Positive Changes in Self-Efficacy as Self-Reported by Students Enrolled from Multiple Colleges of Veterinary Medicine in the United States. Journal of Veterinary Medical Education. 2026.
abstract: In 2025, the American Association of Veterinary Medical Colleges Spectrum of Care Initiative Task Force added spectrum of care (SOC) subcompetencies to their Competency-Based Veterinary Education (CBVE) learning outcomes expected to be achieved by all graduates. This study analyzed the self-reported changes in confidence and self-efficacy of professional veterinary students before and after they completed interactive online coursework aligned with the AAVMCs' SOC subcompetencies related to companion animals. Course content was created using universal design for learning (UDL) principles and offered free of charge to colleges of veterinary medicine (CVMs) accredited by the AVMA Council on Education. Each college determined where, when, and how to insert it into their curriculum. Google Forms was used to collect voluntarily shared data from veterinary students who enrolled from multiple CVMs in the United States. Analysis of de-identified paired pre- and post-course responses from 121 veterinary students showed statistically significant gains for 25 of 26 survey questions that were mapped to the SOC subcompetencies and learning outcomes for companion animals. This study demonstrates that distance education (DE) can be an effective tool for delivering didactic content consistently within the professional veterinary curriculum across multiple CVMs, freeing time for more direct student-to-instructor interaction during clinical rotations where students can apply their SOC skill set. The findings suggest the educational value of including targeted online coursework within the professional veterinary curriculum to teach SOC subcompetencies while meeting accreditation standards of the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) Council on Education regarding DE.

mcqs.q: In 2025, Spectrum of Care (SOC) subcompetencies were added to veterinary curricula learning outcomes expected of all graduates by which body?
o: The American Association of Veterinary Medical Colleges (AAVMC) Spectrum of Care Initiative Task Force
The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH)
mcqs.e: The AAVMC SOC Initiative Task Force added SOC subcompetencies to the Competency-Based Veterinary Education (CBVE) learning outcomes expected of all veterinary graduates.

mcqs.q: A study enrolled 121 veterinary students across multiple U.S. colleges of veterinary medicine in an interactive online Spectrum of Care (SOC) course. What was the main finding regarding student self-efficacy after completing the coursework?
o: Statistically significant self-efficacy gains in 25 of 26 mapped questions
mcqs.e: Paired pre- and post-course responses from 121 students showed statistically significant self-efficacy gains for 25 of the 26 questions mapped to SOC subcompetencies.

mcqs.q: A study of online Spectrum of Care (SOC) coursework delivered to veterinary students across multiple U.S. colleges of veterinary medicine found significant self-efficacy gains. What did the study conclude about distance education as a delivery method for this content?
o: It is ineffective for didactic material
It can consistently deliver didactic SOC content across multiple colleges, freeing clinical time
It violates AVMA Council on Education standards
mcqs.e: Distance education delivered SOC content consistently across multiple colleges while meeting American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) Council on Education accreditation standards, freeing clinical rotation time for direct student–instructor interaction.

title: Clinical Features and Outcomes of Treatment for Effusive Feline Infectious Peritonitis with GS-441524 in Seventeen Retrovirus-Positive Cats
authors: Marilize Van der Walt, Sarah E Jones, Julie K Levy, Emma Hart, Rosa Negash, Wendy M Novicoff, Nicole Jacque, Samantha J M Evans
citation: Marilize Van der Walt, Sarah E Jones, Julie K Levy, Emma Hart, Rosa Negash, Wendy M Novicoff, Nicole Jacque, Samantha J M Evans. Clinical Features and Outcomes of Treatment for Effusive Feline Infectious Peritonitis with GS-441524 in Seventeen Retrovirus-Positive Cats. Pathogens. 2026.
abstract: Background: There is limited information about treatment success and outcomes in retrovirus-positive cats diagnosed with feline infectious peritonitis (FIP). Methods: A survey was distributed to caretakers of cats with feline leukemia virus (FeLV) and/or feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) that were treated with GS-441524 for presumptive effusive FIP based on survey responses. Results: Cats with FIV developed FIP at an older age and longer after retrovirus infection than cats with FeLV. The average starting dosage (7 mg/kg/d) was increased in 65% of cats, and treatment was extended in 35%. Three cats relapsed (18%). There was a 94% (16/17) twelve-week survival rate and 82% (14/17) one-year survival rate. Seven cats were alive at follow-up, a median of 1306 days (range 983-2069) after FIP diagnosis, but many cats succumbed to neoplasia. Conclusions: Treatment success for retrovirus-positive cats with presumptive FIP was similar to previously reported outcomes for FIP alone. This could support current evidence of successful antiviral therapy for similar populations, if noncurrent, unstandardized protocols and unlicensed product use are considered. Additional studies are needed to determine ideal protocols for rapid resolution of FIP, good long-term survival, and limited relapse in retrovirus-positive cats, and the impact of the FeLV proviral load.

mcqs.q: What was the 12-week survival rate for retrovirus-positive cats treated with GS-441524 for presumptive effusive FIP?
mcqs.e: Survival was 94% (16/17) at 12 weeks; 82% (14/17) survived to one year.

mcqs.q: Compared with FeLV-positive cats, FIV-positive cats developed FIP:
o: At a younger age and sooner after infection
At an older age and longer after retrovirus infection
Only in the presence of neoplasia
mcqs.e: FIV cats developed FIP at an older age and a longer interval after retrovirus infection than FeLV cats.

mcqs.q: What was the overall conclusion about treating retrovirus-positive cats for FIP?
o: Therapy is contraindicated in retrovirus-positive cats
Treatment success was similar to outcomes reported for FIP alone
mcqs.e: Outcomes resembled prior FIP-alone results; retrovirus status did not preclude remission, though many cats later died of neoplasia.

title: Feline leukemia virus lifetime study: whole blood samples increase detection of low positive cats with extended long-term survival
authors: Melissa J Beall, Dana Moore, Sean Turner, Julie K Levy
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: Melissa J Beall, Dana Moore, Sean Turner, Julie K Levy. Feline leukemia virus lifetime study: whole blood samples increase detection of low positive cats with extended long-term survival. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2025.
abstract: Objectives: Thousands of cats in the USA are newly diagnosed with feline leukemia virus (FeLV) each year, and known FeLV-infected cats are increasingly adopted from shelters. This study investigated optimal sample types to identify FeLV-infected cats and predictors of long-term survival in a cohort of FeLV-positive cats followed for up to 8 years after diagnosis. Methods: Previously, 127 FeLV p27 antigen-positive cats were enrolled in a prospective study. Whole blood, plasma and serum were collected at enrollment and monthly for 6 months. All sample types were tested on SNAP FIV/FeLV Combo Test (SNAP) monthly, and results from microtiter plate ELISA (PetChek) for p27 antigen and a quantitative RT-PCR (qPCR) for proviral DNA were used for confirmation and classification of infection status (high positive, low positive or cryptic/negative). After the 6-month testing phase, cats entered a lifetime survival monitoring phase. Owner-reported status in the current study extended previous survival results by 4 years. Results: Testing anticoagulated whole blood on SNAP at enrollment identified five and nine more FeLV-infected low positive cats (n = 29) than plasma or serum, respectively. Although some low positive (n = 11) cats demonstrated variable test results on SNAP with plasma and serum, others (n = 17) were SNAP positive with all three sample types and classified as low positive based on PetChek and qPCR results. After an additional 4 years of monitoring, low positive cats had not reached a median survival, with 19/29 (66%) cats still alive compared with 2/90 (2.2%) high positive cats. Conclusions and relevance: Anticoagulated whole blood on SNAP was a sensitive indicator of FeLV infection relative to plasma and serum and therefore should be the preferred diagnostic sample for FeLV antigen testing. Combining the results of whole blood antigen testing, PetChek and qPCR identified cats as high positive, low positive or cryptic/negative, with high positive cats having higher risk for early mortality. Use of these diagnostic tools facilitates the management of FeLV as a chronic condition.

mcqs.q: Which sample type was most sensitive for point-of-care SNAP FeLV antigen testing?
mcqs.e: Whole blood on SNAP detected more low-positive cats than plasma or serum and is the preferred sample.

mcqs.q: How did long-term survival compare between high-positive and low-positive FeLV cats?
o: High-positive cats had higher early mortality while most low-positive cats survived
Low-positive cats died early while high-positive cats survived
mcqs.e: 19/29 (66%) low-positive cats were still alive versus only 2.2% of high-positive cats, which carry high early-mortality risk.

mcqs.q: What is the clinical implication of combining whole-blood antigen, PetChek, and qPCR results?
o: Classifying cats as high/low/cryptic supports managing FeLV as a chronic condition
Adoption of FeLV-positive cats should stop
mcqs.e: Classification into high-, low-positive, or cryptic guides prognosis and supports managing FeLV as a chronic disease.

title: Spectrum of care approach to animal shelter management of feline infectious peritonitis complicated by feline leukemia virus
authors: Emma K LaVigne, Nicole E Levy, Alexis R Bardzinski, Federica Scaletti, Kevin Horecka, Mia K Cuccinello, Dana M Moore, Julie K Levy
citation: Emma K LaVigne, Nicole E Levy, Alexis R Bardzinski, Federica Scaletti, Kevin Horecka, Mia K Cuccinello, Dana M Moore, Julie K Levy. Spectrum of care approach to animal shelter management of feline infectious peritonitis complicated by feline leukemia virus. Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 2025.
abstract: Introduction: Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) occurs most commonly in multi-cat environments such as animal shelters. FIP is often suspected based on compatible history, signalment, physical examination, and hematological and biochemical findings. Increased diagnostic certainty requires additional diagnostic imaging and laboratory testing that may be out of reach for resource-poor caregivers and organizations. The objective of this retrospective study was to evaluate response to GS-441524 (GS) therapy of cats diagnosed with FIP using a spectrum of care approach relying on physical examination, hematology, biochemistry, and Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) antigen at a shelter specializing in the adoption of cats with FeLV. Methods: The FIP treatment protocol included treatment with GS for 84 days, followed by observation for 84 days. Starting dosage, dose adjustment, route of administration, and treatment extensions were based on initial condition and response to therapy. Hematology and biochemistry panels were performed at baseline, treatment, and post-treatment observation periods. Response to treatment and survival times were compared between FeLV-positive and FeLV-negative cats. Results: A total of 170 cats diagnosed with FIP (104 FeLV-positive; 66 FeLV-negative) were included in the study. Hematology and serum chemistry abnormalities and their resolution during treatment were not significantly different between the groups, nor were there significant differences in survival through the treatment period (79% vs. 76%) or observation period (74% vs. 74%) between FeLV-positive and FeLV-negative cats respectively. Most mortality (55%) occurred in the first 7 days; cats surviving >7 days had an 86% survival rate. Despite equivalent responses to GS treatment, the FeLV-positive group experienced progressive mortality following the observation period. Survival of FeLV-positive cats (median 524 days, range 1-1585 days) was significantly shorter than for FeLV-negative cats (median not reached, range 0-1424 days) (p = 0.0001). Fifteen cats (11%) that achieved remission of FIP during the initial treatment experienced one or more episodes of FIP relapse up to 1.2 years later (11 FeLV-positive; 4 FeLV-negative). Discussion: The spectrum of care diagnostic approach appeared to be sufficient and preserved resources for the successful treatment of shelter cats. FeLV-positive cats achieved equivalent FIP remission rates to FeLV-negative cats but were still at risk for shortened lifespan associated with FeLV infection.

mcqs.q: Was a spectrum-of-care diagnostic approach (exam, CBC, chemistry, FeLV antigen, without advanced imaging/PCR) adequate to treat shelter cats for FIP?
o: Yes, it was sufficient and preserved resources
mcqs.e: The spectrum-of-care approach was sufficient to treat shelter FIP with GS-441524 while conserving resources.

mcqs.q: How did FIP remission and treatment-period survival compare between FeLV-positive and FeLV-negative cats?
o: Equivalent FIP remission and treatment-period survival
mcqs.e: Remission rates and treatment-period survival (79% vs 76%) were equivalent between the groups.

mcqs.q: Despite equivalent FIP remission, FeLV-positive cats experienced:
o: Significantly shorter overall survival (median 524 days) from FeLV
mcqs.e: FeLV-positive cats had significantly shorter overall survival driven by underlying FeLV infection, despite equal FIP remission.

title: The impact of free-roaming dogs on lemurs in Madagascar: a decade of research and intervention
authors: Kim Valenta, Tsiky Rajaonarivelo, Angelique Ferreira, Ange Raharinirina, Radoniaina R Rafaliarison, Alisha Farris, Jonas M Watson, Susan deFrance, Dominic Mayo, Caitlynn Filla, Abigail Ross, Sally L Bornbusch, Siddharth Satishchandran, Thomas Kelly, Julie K Levy, Zoavina Randriana, Zach J Farris
citation: Kim Valenta, Tsiky Rajaonarivelo, Angelique Ferreira, Ange Raharinirina, Radoniaina R Rafaliarison, Alisha Farris, Jonas M Watson, Susan deFrance, Dominic Mayo, Caitlynn Filla, Abigail Ross, Sally L Bornbusch, Siddharth Satishchandran, Thomas Kelly, Julie K Levy, Zoavina Randriana, Zach J Farris. The impact of free-roaming dogs on lemurs in Madagascar: a decade of research and intervention. Folia Primatologica. 2025.
abstract: Lemurs are the most endangered group of mammals on earth, and invasive species, including domestic dogs, are considered to be the second greatest threat to biodiversity after habitat loss. Here, we describe and summarize the challenges and results of a decade of research aimed at understanding the impact of dogs on lemurs, and efforts to humanely reduce dog populations in protected areas in Madagascar, to reduce their impact on lemurs and other wildlife, via the non-profit the Mad Dog Initiative. We have found that free-roaming domestic dog populations living in and around Madagascar's protected areas both predate and displace native wildlife, and that the presence of dogs in forests drives a reduction of wildlife in forests. Additionally, dogs vector a number of pathogens that can have lethal consequences for lemur populations, as well as serving as important vectors of anti-microbial resistance. We propose several future directions for research, outreach, and capacity building in Madagascar and other low and middle income countries aimed at better quantifying the threat of domestic species on wildlife, and mitigating its impact.

mcqs.q: According to research on the impact of free-roaming dogs on lemurs in Madagascar, what is considered the second greatest threat to biodiversity after habitat loss?
mcqs.e: Invasive species such as free-roaming domestic dogs are described as the second greatest biodiversity threat after habitat loss.

mcqs.q: How did free-roaming dogs around Madagascar's protected areas affect wildlife?
o: Through predation, displacement, and vectoring pathogens and antimicrobial resistance
mcqs.e: Dogs predated and displaced wildlife and acted as vectors of pathogens and antimicrobial resistance.

mcqs.q: What intervention does the Mad Dog Initiative employ?
o: Humane reduction of free-roaming dog populations
mcqs.e: The Mad Dog Initiative humanely reduces free-roaming dog populations to lessen their impact on lemurs and wildlife.

title: The pandemic's cruel aftermath: progressive decline in spay/neuter capacity
authors: Simone D Guerios, Gina Clemmer, Julie K Levy
citation: Simone D Guerios, Gina Clemmer, Julie K Levy. The pandemic's cruel aftermath: progressive decline in spay/neuter capacity. Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 2025.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic lockdown in early 2020 resulted in a temporary suspension of elective spay and neuter procedures in many low-cost spay/neuter clinics. In our previous study, we projected a deficit of 2.7 million surgeries performed in high-quality high-volume spay-neuter (HQHVSN) clinics as a result of the shutdown and subsequent inability to recover to pre-pandemic productivity by the end of 2021. The purpose of this follow-up study was to determine whether the clinics subsequently recovered and caught up with the previously delayed procedures. Spay-neuter data were collected from 212 HQHVSN clinics from January 2019 through June 2023. The clinics collectively performed 1,217,240 spay/neuter surgeries in the pre-COVID baseline year of 2019. The pandemic triggered a reduction of 13% in 2020, 3% in 2021, 6% in 2022, and 1% in the first half of 2023. Analysis of patient data from the same clinics in our previous report revealed that instead of rebounding to pre-pandemic surgery capacity, they performed even fewer surgeries per quarter in the 18-month follow-up period than they did in 2021. If similar trends occurred in the estimated 3,000 spay-neuter clinics across the United States, the deficit in spay-neuter surgeries is estimated to have risen to 3.7 million surgeries, not including the compounding effect of those intact animals producing litters of their own. The continued decline in low-cost spay-neuter year over year impedes access to basic preventive pet healthcare and threatens to undermine decades of progress in controlling pet overpopulation.

mcqs.q: A follow-up study of 212 high-quality high-volume spay-neuter (HQHVSN) clinics across the United States tracked surgical output through mid-2023. Did HQHVSN clinic spay/neuter capacity rebound after the COVID-19 lockdown?
o: No, it continued to decline and the deficit grew
mcqs.e: Clinics performed even fewer surgeries per quarter in follow-up than in 2021; capacity did not rebound.

mcqs.q: A follow-up study tracking 212 high-quality high-volume spay-neuter (HQHVSN) clinics in the United States through mid-2023 estimated the cumulative spay/neuter deficit since the COVID-19 pandemic. To approximately what figure had the deficit risen (extrapolated to all ~3,000 U.S. spay-neuter clinics)?
mcqs.e: The cumulative deficit was estimated at 3.7 million surgeries, up from the prior 2.7 million projection.

mcqs.q: A 2025 study found a continued year-over-year decline in U.S. low-cost spay/neuter clinic capacity following the COVID-19 pandemic. What do the authors warn this sustained decline threatens?
o: Progress controlling pet overpopulation and access to preventive care
mcqs.e: Continued loss of low-cost spay/neuter undermines pet overpopulation control and access to basic preventive care.

title: Bridging gaps in veterinary care: restructuring a community clinic for cultural inclusion in Phoenix, Arizona
authors: Champayne Danae Master, Marjorie Robin Vincent, Bridgid Ann Twomey, Claudia Vazquez, Jyothi Vinnakota Robertson
citation: Champayne Danae Master, Marjorie Robin Vincent, Bridgid Ann Twomey, Claudia Vazquez, Jyothi Vinnakota Robertson. Bridging gaps in veterinary care: restructuring a community clinic for cultural inclusion in Phoenix, Arizona. Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 2025.
abstract: This case study examines the Arizona Animal Welfare League's (AAWL) efforts to bridge gaps in veterinary care access for Latino communities in Phoenix, AZ, with strategic guidance from JVR Strategies supported by Maddie's Fund. To better understand the specific needs, barriers, and preferences for pet health services, bilingual community needs assessments were conducted through partnerships with PetSmart Charities, Community Alliance Consulting, LLC, the Alliance for Companion Animals Coalition, and the Institute for Human-Animal Connection (IHAC). Insights gained from these needs assessments shaped the restructuring of AAWL's public clinic, leading to the development of a Saturday-only clinic model, bilingual services, outreach, and off-site clinics in targeted zip codes. While the transition posed operational challenges, early results demonstrated increased patient volume, expanded access to care, and created stronger connections with the community. This restructuring created space to listen more deeply to residents through informal conversations and relationship-building in the neighborhoods AAWL sought to serve. Community members consistently pointed to promotoras-local community health workers-as the trusted individuals they already turn to for information, resources, and guidance. Recognizing this, AAWL began building relationships with promotoras, who served as trusted connectors linking community members to AAWL and the veterinary services available to them. This case study examines the organization's process from the initial assessments in 2022 through the clinic's transition to a new model in March 2024, with ongoing adjustments to the model based on community feedback through July 2024. It offers insights into the importance of inclusive needs assessments, community partnerships, and culturally relevant service delivery. These findings provide a framework for organizations aiming to develop community-based veterinary care programs that are both equitable and sustainable.

mcqs.e: Residents pointed to promotoras as trusted sources, so the clinic built relationships with them to link people to care.

title: Key factors in Shelter Veterinary job satisfaction: implications for Access to Veterinary Care in shelters [ABVP conference abstract]
journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health (2025 ABVP Abstracts, Vol. 4 No. S1)
citation: Kate F. Hurley, Janet Scarlett. Key factors in Shelter Veterinary job satisfaction: implications for Access to Veterinary Care in shelters [ABVP conference abstract]. Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health (2025 ABVP Abstracts, Vol. 4 No. S1). 2025.
abstract: Introduction: Extensive negative impacts of the Access to Veterinary Care crisis have been documented in U.S. animal shelters, including prolonged length of stay, reduced adoptions, higher disease levels and increased euthanasia. Simultaneously with developing long term strategies to remedy this crisis, near term solutions are urgently needed. Increasing shelter veterinary job satisfaction and retention could provide some short-term relief as well as being a necessary underpinning of any long-term approach - no amount of newly trained veterinarians will help the sector if shelters are unable to retain these individuals. The authors hypothesized that specific factors linked to shelter veterinary job satisfaction could be identified that would guide shelter leaders and other stakeholders to improve retention of veterinarians already engaged in the field and lay the foundation for more successful recruitment in the future. [This is a published conference abstract; the methods surveyed 94 California shelter veterinarians, with key negative factors for job satisfaction being lack of support staff, inability to meet animals' behavioral needs, and challenging leadership relationships, and the key positive factor being making a meaningful impact. The authors recommend improving retention through operational efficiencies and crowding reduction rather than compensation alone.]

mcqs.q: A survey of 94 California shelter veterinarians examined job satisfaction drivers (published as an ABVP conference abstract). What was identified as the key positive driver of job satisfaction?
mcqs.e: Among 94 California shelter veterinarians, the leading positive factor was making a meaningful impact.

mcqs.q: Which were identified as key negative factors for shelter veterinarian job satisfaction?
o: Lack of support staff, inability to meet animals' behavioral needs, and challenging leadership relationships
mcqs.e: Dissatisfaction was driven by inadequate support staff, inability to meet behavioral needs, and poor leadership relationships.

mcqs.q: Based on a survey of 94 California shelter veterinarians' job satisfaction, how do the study authors recommend improving veterinarian retention?
mcqs.e: They recommend operational efficiencies and crowding reduction rather than relying on compensation alone.

title: Effects of feline personality on pain assessment with two validated behaviour-based scales
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: Ana Cadariu, Chiara Adami. Effects of feline personality on pain assessment with two validated behaviour-based scales. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2025.
abstract: Objectives: The aim of this study was to determine whether feline personality would affect the scores obtained with the Glasgow Feline Composite Measure Pain Scale (CMPS-Feline) and the Feline Grimace Scale (FGS), as well as the mechanical thresholds (MTs), both pre- and postoperatively. Methods: Cats scheduled for elective neutering were included in the study. After at least 12 h of acclimatisation, the cats' personalities were classified, based on the Feline-ality Assessment, as either 'independent' or 'social', always by the same investigator. Then, a second independent investigator assigned FGS and CMPS-Feline scores and measured the MTs with a mechanical algometer before (baseline) and after elective surgical neutering. Either a t-test or Mann-Whitney statistics, depending on data distribution, was used to compare continuous variables between independent and social cats. Results: A total of 29 cats undergoing either orchiectomy or ovariectomy were included in the study. Of them, 14 were classified as independent and 15 as social. Preoperatively, the independent cats had higher CMPS-Feline (2.8 +/- 1.6; P = 0.014) and FGS (0, range 2-1; P = 0.025) scores than the social cats (1.3 +/- 1.2 and 0, range 0-0, respectively). Postoperatively, CMPS-Feline (P = 0.011) and FGS (P = 0.009) scores were higher in the independent cats (3, range 3-5 and 2, range 1-3, respectively) than in the social cats (2, range 1-3 and 1, range 0-1, respectively). MTs did not differ between personality groups either preoperatively or postoperatively. Within personality groups, there were no differences between pre- and postoperative study variables. Conclusions and relevance: Feline personality affects the reliability of both the CMPS-Feline and FGS. This should be considered when these scales are used to assess perioperative pain in clinical cats and to titrate analgesic drugs to effect.

mcqs.q: How did feline personality affect CMPS-Feline and Feline Grimace Scale scores around neutering?
o: 'Independent' cats scored higher than 'social' cats both pre- and postoperatively
'Social' cats scored higher both pre- and postoperatively
mcqs.e: Independent cats had significantly higher CMPS-Feline and FGS scores than social cats at both baseline and after surgery.

mcqs.q: What happened to mechanical thresholds (MTs) between independent and social cats?
o: Did not differ between personality groups
Lower postoperatively in both groups only
mcqs.e: MTs did not differ between personality groups either pre- or postoperatively, despite the scale-score differences.

mcqs.q: What is the practical implication of the findings?
o: Pain scales need no adjustment for temperament
Personality biases scale reliability and should be considered when scoring pain and titrating analgesia
Only mechanical algometry should be used clinically
Social cats require higher analgesic doses
mcqs.e: The authors conclude personality affects reliability of both scales, so it should be accounted for when assessing pain and dosing analgesics.

title: Survey of German veterinarians' approaches to pain assessment and management of perioperative pain in pet rabbits
authors: Stephanie Zein, Katharina C Jensen, Kerstin Muller
citation: Stephanie Zein, Katharina C Jensen, Kerstin Muller. Survey of German veterinarians' approaches to pain assessment and management of perioperative pain in pet rabbits. Veterinary Record. 2025.
abstract: This study aimed to assess veterinary practices in pain recognition and perioperative analgesic therapy in pet rabbits. An online questionnaire was distributed German veterinarians from July to October 2022, containing questions on the frequency with which they treated rabbits and the methods they used to evaluate pain in this species. Additionally, participants were asked detailed questions about their approach to perioperative pain management when performing soft-tissue surgery, specifically an ovariohysterectomy, in rabbits. One hundred and fifty-four questionnaires were considered for final analysis. The most commonly reported indicators to detect pain in rabbits were assessment of food intake and behavioural observation. A total of 23.4% of the participants stated that they used the Rabbit Grimace Scale. Overall, 24.5% of the 110 veterinarians who performed ovariohysterectomies in rabbits reported no use of preoperative analgesia; however, 95.5% administered multimodal analgesia in the pre- and intraoperative phases combined and 60.0% administered analgesia postoperatively. The most commonly mentioned drug combination pre- and postoperatively was metamizole and meloxicam. Opioids and local anaesthetics were used less frequently. The survey had a small sample size and notable selection bias, with 90.3% female participants. Respondents used different indicators to detect pain in rabbits. Analgesic therapy in ovariohysterectomies, as reported by participants, can be considered suboptimal in several cases.

mcqs.q: What proportion of surveyed German veterinarians used the Rabbit Grimace Scale to assess pain?
mcqs.e: Only 23.4% reported using the Rabbit Grimace Scale; food intake and behavioural observation were the most common indicators.

mcqs.q: Regarding preoperative analgesia for rabbit ovariohysterectomy, what did the survey find?
o: Opioids were the most common drugs used
mcqs.e: 24.5% of the 110 vets performing OVH reported no preoperative analgesia, indicating frequently suboptimal practice.

mcqs.q: In a 2022 online survey of German veterinarians about perioperative pain management in pet rabbits undergoing ovariohysterectomy, what was the most commonly reported analgesic drug combination used pre- and postoperatively?
mcqs.e: Metamizole and meloxicam was the most commonly mentioned pre- and postoperative combination.

title: Evaluation of the antiemetic, sedative and analgesic effects of butorphanol and maropitant in combination with dexmedetomidine in cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy
authors: Sitkican Okur, Busra Baykal, Damla T Okur, Taner Arslan, Esra Modoglu, Ayse Golgeli Bedir, Latif E Yanmaz, Ugur Ersoz
citation: Sitkican Okur, Busra Baykal, Damla T Okur, Taner Arslan, Esra Modoglu, Ayse Golgeli Bedir, Latif E Yanmaz, Ugur Ersoz. Evaluation of the antiemetic, sedative and analgesic effects of butorphanol and maropitant in combination with dexmedetomidine in cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy. Veterinary Record. 2025.
abstract: Dexmedetomidine commonly induces emesis in cats, increasing the risk of aspiration and discomfort. Butorphanol and maropitant have been suggested as antiemetic adjuncts, but their comparative efficacy is unclear. Twenty healthy female cats undergoing elective ovariohysterectomy were randomly assigned to receive intravenous dexmedetomidine (25 ug/kg) with either butorphanol (0.2 mg/kg; n = 10) or maropitant (1 mg/kg; n = 10). Incidences of emesis, retching, sialorrhea and lip licking were recorded for 30 minutes, and physiological parameters and sedation scores were assessed at set intervals. The incidence of dexmedetomidine-induced emesis was minimal in cats receiving either butorphanol or maropitant as adjuncts. Butorphanol was associated with deeper early sedation, whereas maropitant was linked to lower postoperative pain scores. Adjunct selection may therefore be tailored according to individual perioperative priorities.

mcqs.q: In cats given dexmedetomidine for ovariohysterectomy, how did butorphanol and maropitant affect emesis?
mcqs.e: Incidence of dexmedetomidine-induced emesis was minimal with either butorphanol or maropitant as an adjunct.

mcqs.q: In a randomized study comparing butorphanol and maropitant as adjuncts to dexmedetomidine in cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy, which adjunct was associated with deeper early sedation?
mcqs.e: Butorphanol was associated with deeper early sedation, whereas maropitant gave lower postoperative pain scores.

mcqs.q: In a randomized study comparing butorphanol and maropitant as adjuncts to dexmedetomidine in cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy, which adjunct was linked to lower postoperative pain scores?
mcqs.e: Maropitant was linked to lower postoperative pain scores, so adjunct choice can be tailored to perioperative priorities.

title: Anesthesia-free dentistry does not provide any demonstrable medical benefit for the control of periodontal disease in dogs
authors: Brook A. Niemiec, Katherine B. Kangas, Erin P. Ribka
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association (JAVMA)
citation: Brook A. Niemiec, Katherine B. Kangas, Erin P. Ribka. Anesthesia-free dentistry does not provide any demonstrable medical benefit for the control of periodontal disease in dogs. Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association (JAVMA). 2026.
abstract: Objective: To determine the effectiveness of anesthesia-free dentistry (AFD) versus anesthetic dentistry for treatment of periodontal disease in dogs. Methods: This prospective study was conducted between April 16, 2014, and October 21, 2014. Client-owned dogs were assigned an initial periodontal diagnostic test strip (PDTS) score (from 0 [white] to 5 [dark yellow]) during conscious oral examination using commercially available rapid test strips to assess salivary concentration of thiols (OraStripdx; PDX Biotech LLC). Eligible dogs included those with a PDTS score >= 3 and no previous dental cleaning (control group, treated with an anesthetized dental procedure) and those with any PDTS score and a history of AFD in the previous 6 weeks (AFD group). Forty-six dogs were enrolled, with 23 in each group. Results: The mean PDTS score was significantly lower at recheck examination after an anesthetized dental procedure (0.087; range, 0 to 1) than after AFD (4.35; range, 3 to 5). Conclusions: AFD provided no demonstrable medical benefit and is not a viable alternative to an anesthetized dental procedure for the mitigation of periodontal disease in dogs.

mcqs.q: A prospective clinical study compared anesthesia-free dentistry (AFD) to anesthetized dental procedures in client-owned dogs with periodontal disease. What was the main conclusion?
o: It is equivalent to anesthetized dentistry
It provided no demonstrable medical benefit and is not a viable alternative
It is superior for early periodontal disease
It is preferred when anesthesia is contraindicated
mcqs.e: AFD provided no demonstrable medical benefit and was not a viable alternative to an anesthetized dental procedure.

mcqs.q: A prospective study compared anesthesia-free dentistry (AFD) to anesthetized dental procedures in dogs using periodontal diagnostic test strip (PDTS) salivary-thiol scores (scale 0–5) as the outcome measure. How did recheck PDTS scores compare between the two groups?
o: Lower after the anesthetized procedure (0.087) than after AFD (4.35)
Lower after AFD than after anesthetized dentistry
Improved only in the AFD group
mcqs.e: Mean PDTS at recheck was 0.087 after the anesthetized procedure versus 4.35 after AFD, showing far better periodontal control with anesthesia.

abstract: This Cat Friendly decision-making document provides guidance on making confident and compassionate end-of-life decisions for cats which are in homing centres or coming through Trap, Neuter, Return (or Relocate; TNR) or community cat neutering programmes. The intended audience is anyone in any country working with, or interested in, unowned cats, principally in the context of cat homing centres (also referred to as shelters, rescues or adoption centres). The document will also be of interest to animal welfare organisations, those undertaking TNR or community cat neutering programmes and veterinary teams working in or with the unowned cat sector.

title: Influence of acepromazine vs. medetomidine on surgical time and complication rate during canine laparoscopic ovariectomy
citation: C. Rennick, et al.. Influence of acepromazine vs. medetomidine on surgical time and complication rate during canine laparoscopic ovariectomy. Journal of Small Animal Practice (JSAP). 2025.
abstract: Objectives: To compare the effect of acepromazine on surgical duration and complication rate when compared to medetomidine during canine laparoscopic ovariectomy. Materials and Methods: In this randomised, prospective clinical study, 32 entire female dogs were randomly assigned to premedication with medetomidine (Group M, n = 20) or acepromazine (Group A, n = 12), with surgery performed by a standardised laparoscopic ovariectomy technique. Results: The mean surgical time from skin incision to removal of both ovaries was 11.8 +/- 1.8 minutes and did not differ significantly between the two groups (M: 11.7 +/- 1.6; A: 11.9 +/- 2.3). Across the entire study population, surgical difficulty was assessed as 'easy' in 14 dogs (44%), 'medium' difficulty in 14 dogs (44%) and 'marked' difficulty in four dogs (12%), while the complication rate was 12.5% in both groups. Clinical Significance: Acepromazine may be used for sedation as part of a balanced premedication protocol as an alternative to medetomidine in dogs undergoing laparoscopic ovariectomy without significantly increasing the procedure time, surgical difficulty or complication rate.

mcqs.e: The complication rate was 12.5% in both groups, with no significant difference in surgical difficulty.

Acepromazine is an acceptable alternative premedication without increasing time or complications

title: When goals align: targeted trap-neuter-(vaccinate)-return project helps students, shelters, cats, and communities
authors: Lena DeTar, Jaclyn Bubnell, M Erin Henry, Daniel Lopez, Jessica Reed
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association (JAVMA)
citation: Lena DeTar, Jaclyn Bubnell, M Erin Henry, Daniel Lopez, Jessica Reed. When goals align: targeted trap-neuter-(vaccinate)-return project helps students, shelters, cats, and communities. Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association (JAVMA). 2026.
abstract: In 2024, Cornell University's Maddie's Shelter Medicine Program, in collaboration with the College of Veterinary Medicine and the local society for the prevention of cruelty to animals (SPCA), launched a service-learning, high-volume trap-neuter-(vaccinate)-return (TNR) initiative at the request of local neighborhood residents to address a chronic community cat crisis and provide needed surgical opportunities for veterinary students. This mixed-methods study investigated the short-term impacts of the project on student surgical experiences, shelter metrics, and community perceptions of human and feline well-being. Through observational and prospective quantitative and qualitative methods, the researchers analyzed changes in student surgical opportunity, shelter cat metrics, and caregiver experiences before and after the 2024 project. During 2024, 147 cats underwent TNR and 48 participating students increased their on-site surgical volume by approximately 3 procedures. Qualitative feedback revealed gains in confidence and perception of professional readiness. Shelter data showed a moderate impact compared to other TNR studies; benefits included a significant reduction in unweaned kittens and a 3-fold reduction in euthanasia from the target community (OR, 3.89; 95% CI, 1.55 to 9.8). A small increase in intake from this neighborhood after intervention reflected better alignment between community needs (fewer) and access to shelter services (more). The largest impact of the project was in the community. Residents reported profound improvements in cat welfare, kitten births, and mortality. They also reported reduced fighting, injuries, and property damage and renewed trust in the local society for the prevention of cruelty to animals. This mixed-methods study demonstrated that a collaborative, service-learning, large-scale TNR intervention generated meaningful benefits for the target community, the local shelter, cats, and veterinary students.
