mcqs.e: T. foetus is a protozoan causing large-bowel disorders, so it belongs on the chronic large-bowel diarrhea differential.

mcqs.q: Which group showed the highest T. foetus prevalence?
mcqs.e: Prevalence was highest (14.9%) in cats under one year of age.

mcqs.q: In a Polish study examining the prevalence of Tritrichomonas foetus in cats presenting with diarrhea, which diagnostic test was used as the method of choice?
mcqs.e: Nested PCR (with modifications to reduce reaction inhibition) was the diagnostic method of choice, detecting T. foetus DNA in 10.6% of 1,606 feline stool samples.

title: Feline Calicivirus Infection: Current Understanding and Implications for Control Strategies
authors: Federica Di Profio, Matteo Carnevale, Fulvio Marsilio, Francesco Pellegrini, Vito Martella, Barbara Di Martino, Vittorio Sarchese
citation: Federica Di Profio, Matteo Carnevale, Fulvio Marsilio, Francesco Pellegrini, Vito Martella, Barbara Di Martino, Vittorio Sarchese. Feline Calicivirus Infection: Current Understanding and Implications for Control Strategies. Animals (Basel). 2025.
abstract: Feline calicivirus (FCV) is a highly contagious pathogen widely circulating in cat populations. FCV has been shown to be able to evade the host immune response through different mechanisms. As a result, following the acute phase of infection, some cats remain persistently infected or experience reinfection cycles with variants of the same strain or with distinct field FCVs. These animals may become asymptomatic carriers, assuming a critical role in virus transmission and posing a significant risk to susceptible cats, particularly in high-density settings. Typical clinical signs of FCV infection include upper respiratory tract disease, oral ulcerations, salivation, and gingivostomatitis. In some cases, FCV infection has also been linked to a range of other clinical manifestations, including severe virulent systemic disease with high mortality rates. Indeed, FCV diversity and evolution have led to the emergence of new genetic, antigenic, and phenotypic variants, challenging disease control. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of FCV, including its molecular biology, epidemiology, pathogenesis and clinical manifestations. Additionally, the role of vaccination and direct prophylaxis is critically evaluated. An integrated approach is essential to mitigate FCV transmission and disease burden in feline populations.

mcqs.q: A hallmark oral clinical sign of feline calicivirus infection is:
mcqs.e: FCV typically causes oral ulceration and gingivostomatitis alongside upper respiratory signs.

mcqs.q: How do persistently infected cats contribute to FCV spread?
o: They become asymptomatic carriers that keep shedding virus
mcqs.e: Persistently infected, often asymptomatic carriers are a key transmission risk in high-density settings.

mcqs.q: Why is vaccination alone insufficient for FCV control?
o: Vaccines themselves cause virulent systemic FCV
mcqs.e: FCV's antigenic diversity and emergence of new variants limit vaccine cross-protection, requiring integrated biosecurity.

title: Evaluating a Response to a Canine Leptospirosis Outbreak in Dogs Using an Owner Survey
citation: Sierra Villanueva, Cord Brundage. Evaluating a Response to a Canine Leptospirosis Outbreak in Dogs Using an Owner Survey. Veterinary Sciences. 2025.
abstract: Leptospirosis is a zoonotic bloodborne infectious disease caused by Leptospira spp. bacteria that infects humans and most mammals, resulting in organ failure and death. A survey presented to dog owners in Los Angeles County communities was conducted in January 2022 following a 2021 outbreak. Of 102 respondents, 90% reported having a primary veterinarian. Results showed 68% were unaware of the outbreak and 77% unfamiliar with leptospirosis signs or its zoonotic nature. Only 22% of dogs were vaccinated against leptospirosis. The data provide insight into dog owners' awareness and perceptions regarding this disease and potential outbreak responses.

mcqs.e: Only 22% of dogs were reported vaccinated against leptospirosis despite the recent outbreak.

o: Most owners were highly familiar with the disease
Most were unaware of leptospirosis signs or its zoonotic nature
All owners had vaccinated their dogs

o: A zoonotic bacterial (spirochete) disease causing organ failure

title: Acute trazodone administration reduces behavioral and physiological indicators of travel-induced anxiety in dogs in a road travel model
authors: Landsberg G, Mendes J, Kosziwka W, Keys DA, Gordon A, King A, Araujo JA, de Rivera C
citation: Landsberg G, Mendes J, Kosziwka W, Keys DA, Gordon A, King A, Araujo JA, de Rivera C. Acute trazodone administration reduces behavioral and physiological indicators of travel-induced anxiety in dogs in a road travel model. Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 2026.
abstract: Travel-induced stress and anxiety are prevalent in dogs and result in behavioral changes that negatively affect well-being. This study assessed whether trazodone or gabapentin could reduce stress during road travel. Thirty-six Beagles received either 10 mg/kg trazodone, 30 mg/kg gabapentin, or placebo two hours before a 10-minute van travel test. Trazodone significantly reduced serum cortisol, lip-licking frequency, global anxiety scores, urination, yawning, and restlessness. Heart rate was higher with trazodone than with gabapentin or control. Gabapentin showed no significant differences versus control. These results support trazodone's stress-alleviating effects for situational use.

mcqs.q: Which drug significantly reduced cortisol and multiple anxiety behaviours in the road-travel model?
mcqs.e: Trazodone 10 mg/kg lowered cortisol, lip-licking, anxiety scores, urination, yawning, and restlessness.

mcqs.q: How did gabapentin 30 mg/kg perform versus placebo?
mcqs.e: Gabapentin showed no significant differences compared with control in this travel model.

mcqs.q: One physiological finding specific to trazodone was:
o: Higher heart rate than gabapentin or control
mcqs.e: Heart rate was higher with trazodone than with gabapentin or control despite reduced behavioural stress.

title: Impact of Living Environment on Attachment Behaviour in Domestic Cats from Private Homes and Shelters
authors: Kappel I, Materne B, Gansloeszer U
citation: Kappel I, Materne B, Gansloeszer U. Impact of Living Environment on Attachment Behaviour in Domestic Cats from Private Homes and Shelters. Animals (Basel). 2025.
abstract: Because cats often struggle to acclimate to laboratory settings, the researchers adapted Ainsworth's Strange Situation Test (SST) for use in environments familiar to the cats. They examined 82 cat-caregiver dyads from private households and animal shelters using a standardised five-phase video procedure with distinct phases of presence, separation, and reunion between cats and their human caregivers. Seven attachment-related behaviours were recorded via focal animal sampling and analysed using mixed models. Significant differences were observed in exploratory behaviour, physical contact, play (social, object, and locomotor), passive behaviour, and vocalisation. Cats from private homes showed more exploratory and play behaviour, particularly after reuniting with their caregiver, indicating a positive influence of the familiar person's presence. Cats from animal shelters showed reduced play behaviour, more passive behaviour, and more frequent purring, particularly following reunion. Physical contact increased following separations, indicating attachment. Meowing was most frequent during absences and reunions, possibly reflecting stress and renewed social contact. Outdoor access emerged as a potential influencing factor for exploratory behaviour. Attachment behaviours in cats were significantly influenced by living environment, outdoor access, and the presence of familiar or unfamiliar individuals.

mcqs.q: Compared with cats from private homes, shelter cats in this Strange-Situation study showed:
o: Reduced play, more passive behaviour, and more frequent purring
mcqs.e: Shelter cats displayed blunted play, increased passivity, and more purring, especially after reunion.

mcqs.e: The authors caution that purring and meowing here may reflect stress, not contentment.

mcqs.q: Which factor emerged as influencing exploratory behaviour?
mcqs.e: Outdoor access was identified as a potential influence on exploratory behaviour.

title: Physiological and Behavioral Evaluation of Shelter Dogs During Veterinary Routine Health Checks
authors: Gazzano V, Curadi MC, Baragli P, Mariti C, Cecchi F, Cavallo S, Sacchettino L, Gazzano A
citation: Gazzano V, Curadi MC, Baragli P, Mariti C, Cecchi F, Cavallo S, Sacchettino L, Gazzano A. Physiological and Behavioral Evaluation of Shelter Dogs During Veterinary Routine Health Checks. Veterinary Sciences. 2025.
abstract: The researchers evaluated stress responses in 26 shelter dogs during routine veterinary examinations, analyzing behavioral scores alongside physiological and hormonal parameters including heart rate, body temperature, cortisol, oxytocin, serotonin, tryptophan, and interleukin-6. A significant negative correlation was observed between oxytocin and cortisol, particularly in dogs exhibiting relaxed behavior. Oxytocin was also negatively correlated with body temperature, supporting a potential role in modulating stress-induced hyperthermia. No significant associations were found between tryptophan, serotonin, interleukin-6, or other physiological measures and behavioral scores. The absence of correlation between tryptophan and serotonin may be due to blood-brain barrier regulation, while interleukin-6's lack of association suggests further investigation is needed. These findings highlight oxytocin's possible buffering effect on the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and suggest that behavioral assessment may offer a more sensitive measure of canine stress than hormonal or physiological parameters alone.

mcqs.q: What relationship was found between oxytocin and cortisol in relaxed shelter dogs?
mcqs.e: Oxytocin correlated negatively with cortisol, particularly in dogs behaving in a relaxed manner.

mcqs.q: What did oxytocin's negative correlation with body temperature suggest?
o: A possible role buffering stress-induced hyperthermia
mcqs.e: The inverse link with body temperature supports oxytocin modulating stress-induced hyperthermia.

mcqs.q: Which measure did the authors suggest may be the most sensitive index of canine stress?
mcqs.e: Behavioural scoring may be more sensitive than single hormonal or physiological measures alone.

title: Participation in a Short-Term Socialization and Training Program Improved Kennel-Raised Dog Welfare
authors: Ing NH, Richardson R, Lamon TK, Daigle CL
citation: Ing NH, Richardson R, Lamon TK, Daigle CL. Participation in a Short-Term Socialization and Training Program Improved Kennel-Raised Dog Welfare. Animals (Basel). 2026.
abstract: Kennel-raised dogs are exposed to more stressors and fewer positive experiences than dogs raised in homes. The authors created a Dog Socialization and Training class to enrich the environment of university teaching dogs. Undergraduate students (103 total) were each assigned a dog (64 total) to socialize and train for at least thirty-six 30-minute periods across 12 weeks. Each student used a Qualitative Behavior Assessment (QBA) tool to score 20 behaviors on a 0-to-125 scale for their dog at the beginning (PRE) and end (POST) of each of nine semesters. PRE QBA scores were high for the ten positive-valence behaviors including Relaxed (75 +/- 6) and low for the ten negative-valence behaviors including Distressed (31 +/- 3). Following the interactive experiences, QBA scores for all 20 behaviors appeared to improve from 9% to 53% (p < 0.006). Principal Component Analysis identified four dimensions responsible for most of the data variance. Providing kennel-housed dogs with regular, positive human interactions was perceived to increase positive valence toward humans and reduce negative responses, with benefits expected to enhance teaching effectiveness, adoptability, and future adaptation to new homes.

mcqs.e: All 20 QBA behaviors improved 9-53% (p<0.006) following the interactive program.

o: High negative-valence and low positive-valence scores
High positive-valence and low negative-valence scores

title: Light quality and time in shelter modulate behavior and cortisol in the domestic cat (Felis catus)
authors: Yaw AM, Gardella ME, Jacobs J, Hoffmann HM
citation: Yaw AM, Gardella ME, Jacobs J, Hoffmann HM. Light quality and time in shelter modulate behavior and cortisol in the domestic cat (Felis catus). iScience. 2025.
abstract: Light is a principal synchronizer of behavior, circadian rhythms, and hormone release patterns, including stress responses. High stress in domestic cats (Felis catus) increases risk of disease, promotes undesirable behaviors, and is associated with reduced adoptions from shelters. To determine how light properties impact stress and behavioral activity patterns in cats, the effects of light intensity and composition were tested in 101 male and female cats using standard, dim, and dim blue-depleted light during the initial five days in a shelter environment. Cats exhibited circadian locomotor activity, peaking at lights-on, in all light conditions. Cortisol levels decreased under dim blue-depleted light versus standard light on day 5. Probability of hiding was only increased in the dim light condition. A behavioral approach test showed declined behavioral stress markers over time in the shelter. The authors demonstrate that indoor light conditions and length of time in shelter modulate stress in cats.

mcqs.q: Compared with standard light, which lighting condition lowered shelter cats' cortisol by day 5?
mcqs.e: Cortisol decreased under dim blue-depleted light versus standard light on day 5.

mcqs.q: An increased probability of hiding occurred only under:
mcqs.e: Hiding probability rose only in the dim, non-blue-depleted condition.

mcqs.q: Over the first days in the shelter, behavioral stress markers in cats:
mcqs.e: A behavioral approach test showed declining stress markers over time in the shelter.

title: Tools for the Approach of Fear, Anxiety, and Stress in the Domestic Feline: An Update
authors: Barrios F, Ruiz P, Damian JP
citation: Barrios F, Ruiz P, Damian JP. Tools for the Approach of Fear, Anxiety, and Stress in the Domestic Feline: An Update. Veterinary Medicine International. 2025.
abstract: Domestic cats are one of the most popular pets worldwide. Despite their growing popularity, there remains a significant gap in understanding their specific needs, leading to frequent challenges in human-cat coexistence and behavioral issues. The distinct emotional systems of cats, compared to other domestic species and humans, complicate the interpretation of feline behavior. Notably, fear, anxiety, and stress are among the most prevalent behavioral problems in cats. This review delves into the core concepts of anxiety, fear, and stress responses in domestic cats, highlighting their unique characteristics and providing recommendations for effective handling. It also presents key international recommendations for creating a 'cat-friendly' environment, as well as suggestions for pharmacological management to ensure a stress-free visit to the clinic for the cat, its caretaker, and the veterinary team.

mcqs.e: The review identifies fear, anxiety, and stress as among the most prevalent feline behavioral problems.

mcqs.q: To reduce stress during veterinary visits, the review recommends:
o: A cat-friendly environment plus pharmacologic management
mcqs.e: It recommends cat-friendly environmental design plus pharmacologic management for a stress-free visit.

mcqs.q: Interpreting feline behavior is complicated because cats:
o: Have emotional systems distinct from other species and humans

title: Comparative analysis of stress markers, metabolic health, and gut microbiota in healthy and disabled dogs in long-term shelters in Thailand
authors: Saengthong A, Brown JL, Towiboon P, Punturee K, Buddhasiri S, Nganvongpanit K, Punyapornwithaya V, Tocharoennirattisai W, Khonmee J
citation: Saengthong A, Brown JL, Towiboon P, Punturee K, Buddhasiri S, Nganvongpanit K, Punyapornwithaya V, Tocharoennirattisai W, Khonmee J. Comparative analysis of stress markers, metabolic health, and gut microbiota in healthy and disabled dogs in long-term shelters in Thailand. PLoS One. 2026.
abstract: Regular welfare assessments are essential for identifying and addressing the physical, behavioral, and emotional needs of shelter dogs, thereby ensuring their well-being and improving chances for adoption or long-term stability. This study compared biomarkers of physiological stress (fecal glucocorticoid metabolites, fGCM), metabolic status (serum malondialdehyde, glucose, triglycerides, LDL and HDL), and fecal microbiota composition over a one-month period in healthy and spinal-injured disabled dogs housed in a large rescue shelter in Thailand for over one year. No significant differences in fGCM concentrations were observed between groups, indicating comparable levels of physiological stress. In contrast, disabled dogs showed significant metabolic and oxidative alterations, including elevated MDA and glucose and lower triglyceride and HDL concentrations. Microbial analyses revealed comparable alpha diversity but differences in beta diversity, with disabled dogs showing a reduced Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio and decreased abundance of beneficial taxa such as Peptostreptococcaceae. The findings suggest that, despite comparable hormonal stress indicators, disabled dogs may experience subclinical physiological shifts warranting more nuanced welfare monitoring, and a multifactorial assessment incorporating metabolic and microbial parameters is recommended for physically impaired shelter dogs.

mcqs.q: Fecal glucocorticoid metabolite (fGCM) levels in disabled versus healthy long-term shelter dogs were:
mcqs.e: No significant fGCM difference was found, indicating comparable physiological stress.

mcqs.q: In a Thai shelter study comparing healthy dogs with spinal-injured (disabled) dogs housed for over one year, which metabolic and oxidative differences were found in the disabled dogs?
o: Elevated malondialdehyde (MDA) and glucose with lower triglyceride and HDL
mcqs.e: Disabled dogs had elevated malondialdehyde (MDA) and glucose and lower triglyceride and HDL concentrations, indicating significant metabolic and oxidative alterations despite comparable hormonal stress levels.

mcqs.q: The authors recommended that welfare assessment of impaired shelter dogs be:
o: Multifactorial, including metabolic and microbial parameters
mcqs.e: They advised multifactorial assessment because cortisol alone missed subclinical metabolic/microbial shifts.

title: Prevalent and Severe Conditions That Compromise the Welfare of Shelter Dogs: Opinions from the Taiwanese Experts
authors: Chen YH, Chen CI, Lin CY, Teng KT
citation: Chen YH, Chen CI, Lin CY, Teng KT. Prevalent and Severe Conditions That Compromise the Welfare of Shelter Dogs: Opinions from the Taiwanese Experts. Animals (Basel). 2025.
abstract: The welfare of shelter dogs is a growing concern, particularly in regions like Taiwan, where public animal shelters often face overcrowding. This study aimed to identify and prioritise welfare conditions affecting shelter dogs in Taiwan's public animal shelters, offering insights into their impacts on population and individual welfare. A modified Delphi approach engaged 14 experts to evaluate the prevalence, severity, and duration of 59 potential welfare conditions using the Five Domains model. The welfare impact of each condition on individual dogs was assessed as the product of severity and duration, with conditions scoring a median of 3 or higher considered critical. Of the 59 identified conditions, 49 were deemed critical. The most prevalent conditions were 'limited access to toys,' 'insufficient foraging opportunities,' and 'intermittent, excessive barking noise.' The most impactful conditions for individual dogs were 'depressive disorders,' 'fear-related or anxiety disorders,' and 'limited space.' The Physical Environment Domain and the Behavioural Interactions Domain were highlighted as having the most significant and prolonged negative effects on welfare. This study provides a comprehensive welfare-condition list for shelter dogs, guiding future welfare improvements and resource allocation.

o: Depressive disorders, fear/anxiety disorders, and limited space
mcqs.e: Depressive disorders, fear/anxiety disorders, and limited space had the greatest individual welfare impact.

mcqs.q: The most prevalent welfare conditions identified were:
o: Limited access to toys, insufficient foraging, and excessive barking
mcqs.e: Limited toy access, insufficient foraging, and excessive barking were the most prevalent conditions.

mcqs.q: Which Five Domains had the most significant prolonged negative welfare effects?
mcqs.e: The Physical Environment and Behavioural Interactions domains drove most welfare harm.

title: The implications of weeklong fostering and co-housing on shelter dog welfare
authors: Gunter LM, Platzer JM, Reed JL, Blade EM, Gilchrist RJ, Barber RT, Feuerbacher EN, Wynne CDL
citation: Gunter LM, Platzer JM, Reed JL, Blade EM, Gilchrist RJ, Barber RT, Feuerbacher EN, Wynne CDL. The implications of weeklong fostering and co-housing on shelter dog welfare. PeerJ. 2026.
abstract: Meeting the needs of dogs in a typical animal shelter can be challenging. Negative environmental inputs such as excessive noise, restrictive kenneling, and social isolation contribute to compromised welfare. Human-animal interaction, such as a temporary stay outside the shelter in a caregiver's home, has been shown to reduce dogs' cortisol levels and increase rest. The authors investigated the impacts of weeklong fostering on dogs' urinary cortisol and activity at two shelters (one open admission, one managed admission), and at the open admission facility a sub-study explored the effects of co-housing before and after foster care. Dogs' urine was collected for cortisol:creatinine analysis and activity monitors were worn for 17 days (five days in the shelter, seven days in a caregiver's home, five days back in the shelter). In total, 84 dogs participated, yielding 1,385 cortisol:creatinine values and 1,205 activity totals. At both shelters, dogs' cortisol decreased and they spent more time resting during weeklong fostering. No significant differences in cortisol or activity were found pre- versus post-fostering, except more mid-intensity activity in the shelter afterward. Housing with versus without another dog did not affect cortisol pre/post foster, but upon reentry to the shelter dogs living with a familiar dog rested more and engaged in less high activity, indicating a positive welfare effect. Significant cortisol and activity differences were also found between the two shelters. A weeklong reprieve from the shelter, and co-housing with a familiar dog upon return, are two evidence-based interventions that can improve shelter dog welfare.

mcqs.q: During the weeklong foster stay, shelter dogs' urinary cortisol and rest:
o: Cortisol fell and they rested more
mcqs.e: At both shelters cortisol decreased and dogs spent more time resting during fostering.

mcqs.q: On return to the shelter, dogs housed with a FAMILIAR dog:
o: Rested more and showed less high-intensity activity
mcqs.e: Co-housing with a familiar conspecific increased rest and reduced high-arousal activity on reentry.

mcqs.q: Comparing pre- versus post-fostering measures in the shelter, the authors found:
o: No significant pre/post difference except more mid-intensity activity
mcqs.e: No significant pre/post cortisol or activity difference was found, aside from more mid-intensity activity afterward.

title: The Development and Piloting of a Quality of Life Assessment Tool for Dogs
citation: Griffin KE, Vinke CM. The Development and Piloting of a Quality of Life Assessment Tool for Dogs. Pets. 2025.
abstract: Assessing dogs' quality of life (QoL) pre- and post-adoption is crucial for shelters and rehoming organisations making decisions with far-reaching consequences for dogs and people. The researchers developed an assessment tool grounded in the Framework of Dogs' Needs, which considers needs at species, breed/breed-type, and individual levels based on scientific literature and expert opinion. The tool comprises three components: participant-completed questionnaires, investigator-administered questionnaires combined with video observations, and participant-recorded videos showing specific canine behaviors. A pilot study involved 14 dog owners who provided feedback on the procedure. The team identified challenges, particularly regarding the feasibility of participant-recorded videos, but participants generally found the time commitment acceptable. Following refinements based on the feedback, the assessment tool is now prepared for deployment in larger-scale research examining canine quality of life throughout the sheltering and rehoming process.

mcqs.q: The dog quality-of-life assessment tool was grounded in:
o: The Framework of Dogs' Needs (species, breed, individual levels)
mcqs.e: The tool was built on the Framework of Dogs' Needs spanning species, breed, and individual levels.

mcqs.q: In piloting a new canine quality-of-life (QoL) assessment tool grounded in the Framework of Dogs' Needs (piloted with 14 dog owners), the main feasibility challenge identified was:
mcqs.e: Feasibility of participant-recorded videos was the key challenge identified; time commitment overall was found to be acceptable by participants.

mcqs.q: A canine quality-of-life (QoL) assessment tool grounded in the Framework of Dogs' Needs — piloted with 14 dog owners and designed for use pre- and post-adoption — comprises how many main components?
mcqs.e: The tool has three components: participant-completed questionnaires, investigator-administered questionnaires combined with video observations, and participant-recorded videos showing specific canine behaviours.

title: Reducing Human-Directed Kennel Reactivity in Shelter-Housed Dogs
citation: Gilchrist RJ, Wynne CDL. Reducing Human-Directed Kennel Reactivity in Shelter-Housed Dogs. Pets. 2025.
abstract: Many stressors have been identified for shelter dogs, and exposure to shelter stressors has been implicated in poor welfare, including the formation of maladaptive behaviors that manifest as unappealing responses toward humans. Inappropriate behavioral reactions to humans lead to longer lengths of stay, so identifying ways to reduce these responses would benefit both the dog's immediate welfare and time to adoption. This study compared response-independent treat delivery (classical counterconditioning, treats delivered regardless of behavior) with a differential-reinforcement-of-other-behavior (DRO) procedure for reducing human-directed kennel reactivity. Both procedures reduced the median percentage of undesirable in-kennel behavior from baseline (decreases of approximately 88% with response-independent treat delivery and 66% with DRO), whereas a control condition increased undesirable behavior by approximately 15%. Response-independent treat delivery offered practical advantages over response-dependent delivery, requiring less time to perform and less skill from the person delivering treats, making it well suited to implementation by shelter staff and volunteers.

mcqs.q: A study comparing interventions for human-directed kennel reactivity in shelter-housed dogs found which procedure produced the larger reduction in undesirable in-kennel behaviour?
mcqs.e: Response-independent treat delivery (classical counterconditioning) cut undesirable behaviour by approximately 88%, outperforming differential-reinforcement-of-other-behaviour (DRO) at ~66%.

title: The impact of delaying behavior rehabilitation onset on fear and outcome measures in dogs in a shelter setting
authors: Collins K, Miller K, Eagan BH, Patterson-Kane E, Rehner-Fleurant T, Cussen V, Reid P
citation: Collins K, Miller K, Eagan BH, Patterson-Kane E, Rehner-Fleurant T, Cussen V, Reid P. The impact of delaying behavior rehabilitation onset on fear and outcome measures in dogs in a shelter setting. Applied Animal Behaviour Science. 2025.
abstract: Fearful dogs in shelters are commonly given a 'settling-in' period before behavior modification begins, but the welfare value of delaying treatment has not been tested. This study compared dogs that began behavior modification soon after intake with dogs whose treatment onset was delayed, evaluating changes in fear and behavioral outcome measures over the course of rehabilitation. Dogs that began behavior modification within approximately ten days of intake showed reductions in fear sooner than dogs whose treatment was delayed. Delaying treatment slightly reduced the total number of weeks spent in treatment, but the prolonged settling-in period without active treatment did not itself improve fear-related behaviors. The authors concluded that, when shelter resources allow, starting behavior modification as early as possible is likely beneficial for the welfare and quality of life of fearful shelter dogs and is the most ethical option, rather than waiting for an extended acclimation period before intervening.

mcqs.e: Early-onset behavior modification reduced fear sooner than a delayed start.

o: Did not itself improve fear-related behaviors
mcqs.e: The extended unsupported acclimation did not by itself improve fear-related behaviors.

o: Never be used in fearful dogs
Begin as early as possible after intake
mcqs.e: Starting behavior modification early was deemed the most beneficial and ethical option.

title: Territorially Stratified Modeling for Sustainable Management of Free-Roaming Cat Populations in Spain: A National Approach to Urban and Rural Environmental Planning
authors: Octavio P. Luzardo, Ruth Manzanares-Fernandez, Jose Ramon Becerra-Carollo, Maria del Mar Travieso-Aja
citation: Octavio P. Luzardo, Ruth Manzanares-Fernandez, Jose Ramon Becerra-Carollo, Maria del Mar Travieso-Aja. Territorially Stratified Modeling for Sustainable Management of Free-Roaming Cat Populations in Spain: A National Approach to Urban and Rural Environmental Planning. Animals (Basel). 2025.
abstract: This study presents the scientific and methodological foundation of Spain's first national framework for the ethical management of community cat populations: the Action Plan for the Management of Community Cat Colonies (PACF), launched in 2025 under the mandate of Law 7/2023. This pioneering legislation introduces a standardized, nationwide obligation for trap-neuter-return (TNR)-based management of free-roaming cats, defined as animals living freely, territorially attached, and with limited socialization toward humans. The PACF aims to support municipalities in implementing this mandate through evidence-based strategies that integrate animal welfare, biodiversity protection, and public health objectives. Using standardized data submitted by 1128 municipalities (13.9% of Spain's total), we estimated a baseline population of 1.81 million community cats distributed across 125,000 colonies. These data were stratified by municipal population size and applied to national census figures to generate a model-ready demographic structure. We then implemented a stochastic simulation using Vortex software to project long-term population dynamics over a 25-year horizon. The model integrated eight demographic-environmental scenarios defined by a combination of urban-rural classification and ecological reproductive potential based on photoperiod and winter temperature. Parameters included reproductive output, mortality, sterilization coverage, abandonment and adoption rates, stochastic catastrophic events, and territorial carrying capacity. Under current sterilization rates (~20%), our projections indicate that Spain's community cat population could surpass 5 million individuals by 2050, saturating ecological and social thresholds within a decade. In contrast, a differentiated sterilization strategy aligned with territorial reproductive intensity (50% in most areas, 60-70% in high-pressure zones) achieves population stabilization by 2030 at approximately 1.5 million cats, followed by a gradual long-term decline. This scenario prioritizes feasibility while substantially reducing reproductive output, particularly in rural and high-intensity contexts. The PACF combines stratified demographic modeling with spatial sensitivity, offering a flexible framework adaptable to local conditions. It incorporates One Health principles and introduces tools for adaptive management, including digital monitoring platforms and standardized welfare protocols. While ecological impacts were not directly assessed, the proposed demographic stabilization is designed to mitigate population-driven risks to biodiversity and public health without relying on lethal control. By integrating legal mandates, stratified modeling, and realistic intervention goals, this study outlines a replicable and scalable framework for coordinated action across administrative levels. It exemplifies how national policy can be operationalized through data-driven, territorially sensitive planning tools. The findings support the strategic deployment of TNR-based programs across diverse municipal contexts, providing a model for other countries seeking to align animal welfare policy with ecological planning under a multi-level governance perspective.

mcqs.e: At ~20% coverage, the model projects the population could exceed 5 million by 2050.

mcqs.e: The differentiated strategy stabilized the population by 2030 at about 1.5 million.

title: Comprehensive Evaluation and Future Perspectives of Non-Surgical Contraceptive Methods in Female Cats and Dogs
authors: Sheila I. Pena-Corona, Melissa Aurea Vaquera-Guerrero, Jose Cerbon-Gutierrez, Juan I. Chavez-Corona, Adrian E. Iglesias-Reyes, Alonso Sierra-Resendiz, Juan Jose Perez-Rivero, Socorro Retana-Marquez, Pablo Adrian Vizcaino-Dorado, David Quintanar-Guerrero, Gerardo Leyva-Gomez, Dinorah Vargas-Estrada
citation: Sheila I. Pena-Corona, Melissa Aurea Vaquera-Guerrero, Jose Cerbon-Gutierrez, Juan I. Chavez-Corona, Adrian E. Iglesias-Reyes, Alonso Sierra-Resendiz, Juan Jose Perez-Rivero, Socorro Retana-Marquez, Pablo Adrian Vizcaino-Dorado, David Quintanar-Guerrero, Gerardo Leyva-Gomez, Dinorah Vargas-Estrada. Comprehensive Evaluation and Future Perspectives of Non-Surgical Contraceptive Methods in Female Cats and Dogs. Animals (Basel). 2025.
abstract: The issue of stray cats and dogs is a global concern with considerable implications for animal welfare and public health. This review aims to provide an updated and comprehensive analysis of non-surgical contraceptive methods tested in studies controlled in vivo in feline and canine females. Immunocontraception via vaccination against gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the luteinizing hormone receptor, zona pellucida proteins, and sperm, or use of viral-vectored delivery, is yet developing. Hormonal treatment (progestins, androgens, or GnRH) analogs act directly to block the reproductive axis. However, it produced essential side effects. Analogs of kisspeptin, non-steroid anti-inflammatory drugs such as firocoxib, and delivery of cytotoxins to the pituitary have shown non-conclusive results. Additional methods have also been tested, such as intraovarian injection of necrosing compounds or intravaginal and intrauterine devices. At present, neither of these methods offers permanent sterility that can replace surgical sterilization techniques. To our knowledge, none are currently authorized by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) or the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for contraceptive methods or sterilization of cats or dogs. Therefore, it is necessary to continue the development of a compound that warrants the sterility of cats and dogs.

mcqs.q: The review concluded that current non-surgical contraceptives:
o: Offer permanent sterility in dogs only
Do not yet provide permanent sterility able to replace surgery
mcqs.e: No non-surgical method yet offers permanent sterility able to replace surgical spay.

mcqs.q: According to a comprehensive review of non-surgical contraceptive methods in female cats and dogs, regarding regulatory approval these methods are currently:
o: Approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
Approved by neither the FDA nor the European Medicines Agency (EMA)
mcqs.e: None of the reviewed non-surgical contraceptive methods are currently authorised by the FDA or the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for cats or dogs.

mcqs.q: Immunocontraceptive approaches reviewed for non-surgical sterilisation in female cats and dogs target antigens including:
o: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the luteinizing hormone (LH) receptor, and zona pellucida proteins
mcqs.e: Immunocontraception targets GnRH, the LH receptor, zona pellucida proteins, and sperm antigens, with some approaches using viral-vectored delivery.

title: Changes in free-roaming dog population demographics and health associated with a catch-neuter-vaccinate-release program in Jamshedpur, India
authors: Lauren Margaret Smith, Tamara Kartal, Sanjay Rawat, Amit Chaudhari, Ashok Kumar, Rajesh Kumar Pandey, Rupert Julian Quinnell, Lisa M. Collins
citation: Lauren Margaret Smith, Tamara Kartal, Sanjay Rawat, Amit Chaudhari, Ashok Kumar, Rajesh Kumar Pandey, Rupert Julian Quinnell, Lisa M. Collins. Changes in free-roaming dog population demographics and health associated with a catch-neuter-vaccinate-release program in Jamshedpur, India. PLOS One. 2025.
abstract: India's large free-roaming dog populations contribute to significant human health, environmental, and social challenges. Population management strategies, such as catch-neuter-vaccinate-release (CNVR), aim to reduce dog numbers, improve their welfare, and reduce human-animal conflict. Humane Society International (HSI; now operating as Humane World for Animals), in partnership with the Animal Health Foundation, implemented a CNVR program in Jamshedpur, neutering and vaccinating over 20,000 dogs. This study evaluated the impact of this program on dog health, population structure and size. The study areas encompassed 10 sites within Jamshedpur, including both intervention sites where CNVR was directly applied and sites without direct intervention. Data was collected from May 2014 until December 2018, including bi-annual street surveys, as well as clinical data from the dogs captured and treated. We fit logistic regression, negative binomial, and binomial mixed effects models to assess changes in dog population characteristics, health, and reproductive conditions over time in relation to the CNVR intervention. We found that, over the period of this study, the probability of dogs entering the clinic with mange, transmissible venereal tumours, and pregnant significantly reduced. Street surveys showed an increase in sterilised dogs, with higher proportions observed in CNVR-treated sites, although the counts of dogs observed increased overall. The age-structure of free-roaming dogs remained stable over time. In CNVR-treated areas, the probability of observing lactating female dogs decreased, whereas it increased in untreated sites. This work contributes to the growing body of knowledge investigating the impact of dog population management interventions. Continued monitoring and evaluation of CNVR programs are required to identify optimal coverage required to reduce population size effectively.

mcqs.q: A catch-neuter-vaccinate-release (CNVR) program in Jamshedpur, India neutered and vaccinated over 20,000 free-roaming dogs. Following the program, the probability of dogs presenting with mange, transmissible venereal tumour, or pregnancy:
mcqs.e: These health and reproductive markers significantly declined over the course of the CNVR program, demonstrating improved individual dog welfare.

mcqs.q: In a study evaluating a catch-neuter-vaccinate-release (CNVR) programme for free-roaming dogs in Jamshedpur, India, overall street counts of observed dogs:
o: Increased overall despite a higher proportion of sterilised dogs
mcqs.e: The proportion of sterilised dogs rose in CNVR-treated sites, but overall observed dog counts increased, indicating that the coverage achieved was insufficient to reduce the free-roaming dog population.

mcqs.q: A study evaluating a catch-neuter-vaccinate-release (CNVR) program for free-roaming dogs in India found improved welfare but no reduction in overall dog counts. The findings suggest CNVR reduces population size only when coverage:
o: Is high enough to outpace recruitment and immigration
mcqs.e: Welfare improved without population reduction, demonstrating that coverage must exceed reproductive recruitment and immigration rates to shrink an open free-roaming dog population.

title: Managing free-roaming domestic dog populations using surgical sterilisation: a randomised controlled trial
authors: H. R. Fielding, K. A. Fernandes, Amulya V. R., D. Belgayer, A. Misquita, R. Kenny, A. D. Gibson, L. Gamble, B. M. C. Bronsvoort, R. J. Mellanby, I. Handel, D. Rivett, K. Newman, R. King, I. Sayyed, A. Sayed, K. Lad, M. Yaraguda, A. D. Parate, M. K. Balagali, S. Mazeri
citation: H. R. Fielding, K. A. Fernandes, Amulya V. R., D. Belgayer, A. Misquita, R. Kenny, A. D. Gibson, L. Gamble, B. M. C. Bronsvoort, R. J. Mellanby, I. Handel, D. Rivett, K. Newman, R. King, I. Sayyed, A. Sayed, K. Lad, M. Yaraguda, A. D. Parate, M. K. Balagali, S. Mazeri. Managing free-roaming domestic dog populations using surgical sterilisation: a randomised controlled trial. Scientific Reports. 2025.
abstract: Free-roaming domestic dogs (FRDs) are among the most abundant carnivores on earth and have coexisted with humans for over 15,000 years, yet increases in negative interactions and the transmission of zoonotic diseases, precipitates calls for population management. Despite significant investment in FRD sterilisation in India, where rabies is endemic, there is limited evidence of its impact on reducing FRD population sizes. Therefore, robust evaluation of the effectiveness of fertility control programmes is necessary. To address this, we implemented a Before After Control Intervention (BACI) framework in the first multi-site randomised controlled trial for the sterilisation of FRDs. We conducted single intensive sterilisation campaigns in five areas, achieving female sterilisation coverages of 58-66%. We observed a decrease in puppies and lactating females and a reduction in residents' reports of barking, a common problem associated with FRDs. There were no significant differences in adult FRD counts between intervention and control sites during the 2-year follow-up. However, unmeasured immigration into and emigration out of study areas may have confounded counts. One-off, albeit intense, sterilisation campaigns in open populations require substantial investment and are unlikely to reduce population size in isolation, though there may be some reduction in problematic behaviours and improved animal welfare.

mcqs.q: In the first multi-site RCT of free-roaming dog sterilization (58-66% female coverage), what happened to adult dog counts over 2 years?
o: No significant difference vs control sites
mcqs.e: Despite high female coverage, adult FRD counts did not differ from controls, likely confounded by immigration in open populations.

mcqs.q: Which benefits DID the single intensive campaign produce?
o: Fewer puppies, fewer lactating females, less nuisance barking
mcqs.e: The campaign reduced puppies, lactating females, and barking complaints even without lowering adult counts.

mcqs.q: What is the key lesson for one-off sterilization in open populations?
o: A single campaign reliably halves the population
Sustained, repeated effort is needed; one-off campaigns are unlikely to reduce size
mcqs.e: Intense single campaigns require heavy investment but won't shrink open populations alone; ongoing effort is required.

title: Optimizing dog population control strategies in Thailand using mathematical and economic modeling
authors: Weerakorn Thichumpa, Anuwat Wiratsudakul, Saranath Lawpoolsri, Yanin Limpanont, Weerapong Thanapongtharm, Lauren M. Smith, Sarawut Maneewong, Wirichada Pan-ngum
citation: Weerakorn Thichumpa, Anuwat Wiratsudakul, Saranath Lawpoolsri, Yanin Limpanont, Weerapong Thanapongtharm, Lauren M. Smith, Sarawut Maneewong, Wirichada Pan-ngum. Optimizing dog population control strategies in Thailand using mathematical and economic modeling. PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 2025.
abstract: A mathematical model was constructed to investigate dog population dynamics and explore the impact of population management and rabies prevention. We aimed to evaluate cost-effective sterilization and vaccination strategies for dog population control and rabies prevention in Thailand. The developed compartmental model was calibrated with dog population data from Lopburi province (between 2019 and 2022) and simulated five sterilization scenarios. These measures included a combined 80% coverage of the rabies vaccine and 20% coverage of a sterilization program among non-specific dog types. Our findings indicated that sterilization programs targeting female indoor, outdoor, and stray dogs may prove to be the most effective in reducing the total dog population above 50% over a five-year period, surpassing the efficacy of the current intervention. Furthermore, the cost-effectiveness analysis showed that the two female dog sterilization strategies were cost-saving compared to the current practice, as the total costs of sterilization and vaccination decreased over time due to the reduction in the dog population. In conclusion, targeting female dog sterilization could reduce the population and was cost-saving compared to current strategies. Further data to inform dog population demographic and available resources including manpower, rabies vaccine, sterilization toolkits, and related materials will be required to fully explore intervention accessibility and feasibility within the context of rabies prevention and control in Thailand.

mcqs.q: Per the Thailand model, which sterilization strategy most reduced the total dog population?
o: Targeting female dogs across indoor/outdoor/stray classes
mcqs.e: Female-targeted sterilization across all classes cut the total population by >50% over 5 years.

mcqs.q: How did the two female-sterilization strategies compare on cost vs current practice?
o: Cost-saving over time as the population declined
mcqs.e: Total sterilization/vaccination costs fell as the population shrank, making female-focused programs cost-saving.

mcqs.q: What rabies vaccine coverage was modeled alongside sterilization?
mcqs.e: The integrated scenario paired 80% rabies vaccine coverage with sterilization for rabies prevention.

title: The Impact of Catch-Neuter-Vaccinate-Return (CNVR) on Greater Bangkok Residents' Attitudes and Behaviours Towards Free-Roaming Dogs
authors: Elly Hiby, Tuntikorn Rungpatana, Alicja Izydorczyk, Valerie Benka, Craig Rooney
citation: Elly Hiby, Tuntikorn Rungpatana, Alicja Izydorczyk, Valerie Benka, Craig Rooney. The Impact of Catch-Neuter-Vaccinate-Return (CNVR) on Greater Bangkok Residents' Attitudes and Behaviours Towards Free-Roaming Dogs. Animals (Basel). 2025.
abstract: Between 2016 and 2023, over 400,000 dogs in Greater Bangkok, Thailand, were sterilised and vaccinated against rabies through a Catch, Neuter, Vaccinate, Return (CNVR) programme. CNVR is practiced in many countries to humanely and effectively manage free-roaming dog populations, and to mitigate canine and human rabies risks. Residents were surveyed about their experiences, attitudes, and behaviours towards free-roaming dogs. Responses were evaluated in relation to respondents' dog ownership status and the CNVR intensity within their local administrative area (0, 1, 2, or 3 CNVR rounds). The results show an overall positive effect of CNVR. A dose-dependent CNVR effect was observed with residents' perceptions of declines in free-roaming dog populations and puppies born in their community, as well as in being troubled by free-roaming dogs now versus before the intervention. Residents living in areas with the highest levels of CNVR also had lower odds of reporting a dog bite. Some measures, including other current attitudes and behaviours towards free-roaming dogs, did not exhibit this dose-dependent effect. Dog owners showed higher levels of tolerance and care for street dogs than non-owners. The results suggest that owned dogs contributed substantially to the roaming dog population and must be considered in management efforts. CNVR appears to have delivered meaningful benefits to Greater Bangkok residents, and the majority reported sterilisation as their preferred management approach.

mcqs.q: A survey evaluated Greater Bangkok residents' perceptions of free-roaming dog populations after a Catch-Neuter-Vaccinate-Return (CNVR) programme. What effect pattern did CNVR intensity have on residents' perceptions?
o: No effect at any CNVR level
Dose-dependent: more CNVR rounds correlated with fewer perceived roaming dogs/puppies and lower odds of dog bite
An inverse effect (more rounds, worse perceptions)
Benefit observed only for dog owners
mcqs.e: The Bangkok CNVR survey found a dose-dependent effect: residents in areas receiving more CNVR rounds reported greater perceived population declines and lower odds of reporting a dog bite.

mcqs.q: A Catch-Neuter-Vaccinate-Return (CNVR) programme in Greater Bangkok (2016–2023), which sterilised over 400,000 free-roaming dogs, identified a key source of ongoing population pressure. What did the survey conclude about owned dogs?
o: Owned dogs are irrelevant to street dog populations
Owned, free-roaming dogs contribute substantially and must be included in management efforts
Only stray-born dogs maintain street populations
mcqs.e: The Greater Bangkok CNVR survey found that owned dogs roaming freely were substantial contributors to the street dog population; responsible-ownership measures must therefore be integrated alongside CNVR.

mcqs.q: Which management approach did most residents prefer?
mcqs.e: The majority reported sterilisation as their preferred free-roaming dog management approach.

title: Advancing and Historical Reversible Contraceptive Solutions for Feline Reproductive Control
citation: Lluis Ferre Dolcet. Advancing and Historical Reversible Contraceptive Solutions for Feline Reproductive Control. Reproduction in Domestic Animals. 2025.
abstract: Medical approaches to reproduction control have traditionally relied on progestins, but these drugs are associated with significant adverse effects in both males and females, including an increased risk of uterine infections, mammary tumours, and metabolic complications. As a result, veterinarians often advocate for strategies such as postponing estrus in females to balance reproductive health and manage population control. In recent decades, advancements in pharmacological interventions have opened new doors. GnRH agonists, which can reversibly suppress reproductive function, have emerged as a safer and more flexible alternative to surgical sterilisation. Similarly, the use of melatonin in female cats has shown promising results in regulating estrus cycles. Other innovative solutions, such as non-surgical sterilisation techniques using immunocontraceptive vaccines, are under active development, offering hope for scalable, humane population control measures. These emerging technologies provide veterinarians with an expanding toolkit to address both clinical and ethical challenges in reproductive management.

mcqs.q: Why are progestins no longer the preferred feline contraceptive?
o: They risk uterine infection, mammary tumors, and metabolic complications
mcqs.e: Progestins carry significant adverse effects including pyometra, mammary tumors, and metabolic problems.

mcqs.q: Which reversible agent is highlighted as a safer alternative to surgical sterilization?
mcqs.e: GnRH agonists reversibly suppress reproduction and are a safer, more flexible alternative to spay.

mcqs.q: What is the status of feline immunocontraceptive vaccines per the abstract?
mcqs.e: Immunocontraceptive vaccines are an emerging, still-developing technology offering scalable hope.

title: Gene therapy with feline anti-Mullerian hormone analogs disrupts folliculogenesis and induces pregnancy loss in female domestic cats
authors: William A. Stocker, Lauren Olenick, Shreya Maskey, Denise Skrombolas, Haitong Luan, Sophie G. Harrison, Matt Wilson, Anne Traas, Mark Heffernan, Samantha Busfield, Kelly L. Walton, Craig A. Harrison
citation: William A. Stocker, Lauren Olenick, Shreya Maskey, Denise Skrombolas, Haitong Luan, Sophie G. Harrison, Matt Wilson, Anne Traas, Mark Heffernan, Samantha Busfield, Kelly L. Walton, Craig A. Harrison. Gene therapy with feline anti-Mullerian hormone analogs disrupts folliculogenesis and induces pregnancy loss in female domestic cats. Nature Communications. 2025.
abstract: For female domestic cats, ovariohysterectomy is the only method of inducing permanent infertility. However, hundreds-of-millions of free-roaming cats globally highlight the necessity for alternative contraceptive approaches. One strategy involves a single injection of vector delivering a fertility-inhibiting protein for lifetime contraception. Recent studies in mice and cats have identified anti-Mullerian hormone as an excellent candidate for this type of contraception. Here, we leverage our recent characterization of the molecular mechanisms underlying human anti-Mullerian hormone synthesis and activity, to generate potent feline anti-Mullerian hormone analogs. Single intramuscular delivery of these analogs to female cats using an adeno-associated viral vector leads to a greater than 1000-fold increase in feline anti-Mullerian hormone levels, which are sustained for 9 months. High serum anti-Mullerian hormone is associated with abnormal estrus cyclicity, non-follicular ovarian cyst formation, and a progressive decline in antral follicle numbers, however, the few surviving large follicles continue to ovulate. Unlike previous studies, supraphysiologic levels of anti-Mullerian hormone do not block conception, although they are incompatible with the maintenance of pregnancy. Our findings highlight the complexity of the effects of anti-Mullerian hormone on ovarian physiology but confirm that this growth factor is a candidate for fertility control in free-roaming cats.

mcqs.q: A gene therapy study in adult female cats used a single intramuscular injection of an adeno-associated viral (AAV) vector delivering a feline anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) analog. What was the effect on conception versus pregnancy maintenance?
o: Did not block conception but was incompatible with maintaining pregnancy
mcqs.e: Despite supraphysiologic AMH levels, conception was not blocked; however, elevated AMH was incompatible with maintaining pregnancy — an important limitation for this fertility-control candidate.

mcqs.q: In a feline gene therapy contraception study, a single intramuscular injection of an adeno-associated viral vector raised feline anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) levels more than 1000-fold. How long were these elevated AMH levels sustained?
mcqs.e: A single IM dose of the AAV-delivered AMH analog raised serum AMH over 1000-fold, with levels sustained for approximately 9 months, demonstrating a prolonged effect from a single administration.

mcqs.q: In a feline gene therapy contraception study, sustained supraphysiologic anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) levels were induced by a single viral vector injection in adult female cats. What ovarian changes accompanied these high AMH levels?
o: Abnormal estrus cyclicity, non-follicular ovarian cyst formation, and declining antral follicle numbers
mcqs.e: High AMH caused abnormal estrus cyclicity, non-follicular cyst formation, and progressive decline in antral follicle counts, though the few surviving large follicles continued to ovulate.

title: Gene therapy delivery of anti-Mullerian hormone in prepubertal female domestic cats induces long-term sterilization
authors: Philippe Godin, Nicholas Nagykery, Natalie Sicher, Julie L. Barnes, Amy G. Miller, Christina Bunner, Amy K. Thompson, Motohiro Kano, Guangping Gao, Dan Wang, Patricia K. Donahoe, Linda Rhodes, David A. Brake, Thomas J. Conlon, William F. Swanson, Lindsey M. Vansandt, David Pepin
citation: Philippe Godin, Nicholas Nagykery, Natalie Sicher, Julie L. Barnes, Amy G. Miller, Christina Bunner, Amy K. Thompson, Motohiro Kano, Guangping Gao, Dan Wang, Patricia K. Donahoe, Linda Rhodes, David A. Brake, Thomas J. Conlon, William F. Swanson, Lindsey M. Vansandt, David Pepin. Gene therapy delivery of anti-Mullerian hormone in prepubertal female domestic cats induces long-term sterilization. Nature Communications. 2025.
abstract: The uncontrolled reproduction of free-roaming domestic cats exacerbates their welfare challenges and the ecological pressure they exert on wildlife populations. Because of logistic and economic constraints, surgical sterilization alone cannot scale to control the reproduction of the hundreds of millions of intact cats worldwide. Herein, we report that the single administration of an adeno-associated viral vector delivering an anti-Mullerian hormone transgene to prepubertal cats can fully prevent pregnancy once females reach adulthood. Treated kittens were closely monitored for up to 21 months to assess long-term health, transgene expression, reproductive hormones, and reproductive function. The intramuscular injection was well tolerated and did not impact physical growth. The sustained expression of anti-Mullerian hormone did not impact spermatogenesis in males. However, it induced sterility in mated females by preventing breeding-induced ovulation and increases in progesterone associated with luteal phases, resulting in safe and potentially lifetime sterilization in the female domestic cat.

mcqs.q: In a gene therapy study for feline fertility control, prepubertal female kittens received a single intramuscular injection of an adeno-associated viral (AAV) vector delivering an anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) transgene. What was the contraceptive outcome once females reached adulthood?
o: Follicle loss only, without preventing pregnancy
mcqs.e: A single prepubertal AAV-AMH injection fully prevented pregnancy in mated adult females monitored for up to 21 months, representing potentially lifetime sterilization.

mcqs.q: By what mechanism was sterility induced in mated females?
o: Preventing breeding-induced ovulation and the luteal progesterone rise
mcqs.e: Sustained AMH blocked breeding-induced ovulation and luteal-phase progesterone, causing sterility.

mcqs.q: What was the effect on male spermatogenesis and physical growth?
mcqs.e: The injection was well tolerated, sparing male spermatogenesis and not impacting growth.

title: Influence of gonadectomy and age at gonadectomy on the risk of developing intervertebral disc herniation in French Bulldogs: a retrospective study
authors: Marco Tabbi, Alessandro Troisi, Domenico Fugazzotto, Romina Marcoccia, Giorgia Pettina, Simone Minniti, Girolamo Messina, Temy Coppola, Gaetano Principato, Federica Arrigo, Giuseppe Barillaro, Daniele Troiano, Angela Polisca, Viola Zappone
citation: Marco Tabbi, Alessandro Troisi, Domenico Fugazzotto, Romina Marcoccia, Giorgia Pettina, Simone Minniti, Girolamo Messina, Temy Coppola, Gaetano Principato, Federica Arrigo, Giuseppe Barillaro, Daniele Troiano, Angela Polisca, Viola Zappone. Influence of gonadectomy and age at gonadectomy on the risk of developing intervertebral disc herniation in French Bulldogs: a retrospective study. Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 2025.
abstract: The French Bulldog has become increasingly popular worldwide, but selective breeding for brachycephalic traits has increased its predisposition to several neurological disorders. Among these, intervertebral disc herniation (IVDH) is one of the most common causes of spinal cord compression, pain, and neurological deficits. Although genetic predisposition plays a key role, previous evidence suggests that gonadal hormones factors may also adversely affect skeletal development and spinal biomechanics, thus influencing risk of IVDH. The aim of this study is to evaluate the influence of gonadectomy and age at gonadectomy on the risk of developing IVDH in French Bulldogs. Medical records of 2,101 French Bulldogs were retrospectively reviewed. Dogs with complete clinical and reproductive histories were included and classified into two groups: affected (A group, with IVDH) and control (C group, without IVDH). Early-gonadectomized dogs (<12 months) showed a significantly higher risk of IVDH compared with intact dogs. Early-gonadectomized males were nearly twice as likely to develop IVDH (OR = 1.92) than intact males, while early-gonadectomized females exhibited an even stronger association (OR = 9.84) compared with late-gonadectomized (OR = 2.77) and intact females. The preliminary results of this study suggest a potential influence of gonadectomy and age at gonadectomy on the risk of developing IVDH in French Bulldog. Therefore, the age at which gonadectomy is performed should be carefully considered in this and other predisposed chondrodystrophic breeds. These findings highlight the importance of gonadal hormones and the need for further research to evaluate the differential effects of early age gonadectomy.

mcqs.q: How did early gonadectomy (<12 months) affect intervertebral disc herniation risk in French Bulldogs?
mcqs.e: Early-gonadectomized dogs had significantly higher IVDH risk than intact dogs.

mcqs.q: In a retrospective study of 2,101 French Bulldogs examining gonadectomy timing and intervertebral disc herniation (IVDH) risk, which group had the strongest association with IVDH?
mcqs.e: Early-gonadectomized (before 12 months) females had the largest odds ratio for IVDH (OR 9.84) compared with intact females — the strongest association observed in any group.

mcqs.q: A retrospective study of 2,101 French Bulldogs found that early gonadectomy (before 12 months) significantly increased the risk of intervertebral disc herniation compared with intact dogs. What was the main clinical implication?
o: Always neuter French Bulldogs before 6 months
Carefully consider and potentially delay gonadectomy timing in predisposed chondrodystrophic breeds
Gonadectomy timing is irrelevant to disc herniation risk
mcqs.e: The findings highlight that gonadal hormones influence spinal biomechanics; veterinarians should carefully weigh gonadectomy timing in chondrodystrophic breeds prone to intervertebral disc herniation.

title: Cumulative gonadal hormone exposure is nonlinearly associated with risk of canine cranial cruciate ligament disease: a generalised additive model analysis of 20,590 dogs (1988-2023)
citation: D. Low. Cumulative gonadal hormone exposure is nonlinearly associated with risk of canine cranial cruciate ligament disease: a generalised additive model analysis of 20,590 dogs (1988-2023). Journal of Small Animal Practice. 2025.
abstract: Objectives: To investigate the association between cumulative gonadal hormone exposure and the risk of cranial cruciate ligament disease (CrCLD) in dogs. Materials and Methods: Secondary analysis of retrospective cohort data of 20,590 dogs (9845 female, 10,745 male) investigating the association between age at gonadectomy and various health outcomes in dogs was conducted. Cumulative gonadal hormone exposure was defined as the continuous independent variable. The occurrence of CrCLD was binarily defined as the outcome measure. Generalised additive models were used to assess the relationship between hormone exposure and risk of CrCLD, adjusted for potential confounders. Results: The prevalence of CrCLD was 245 of 9845 (2.49%) in females and 203 of 10,745 (1.89%) in males. The risk of CrCLD was nonlinearly associated with cumulative gonadal hormone exposure in both sexes. The risk of CrCLD was greatest in dogs with the least gonadal hormone exposure, sharply decreasing to minima at 1054 days for females and 805 days for males. Clinical Significance: Risk of CrCLD is nonlinearly associated with age at gonadectomy in dogs. Early gonadectomy may be preliminarily defined as that before 2.9 and 2.2 years in female and male dogs, respectively, in the context of CrCLD risk.

mcqs.q: Cranial cruciate ligament disease risk was greatest in dogs with which hormone exposure?
mcqs.e: Risk was highest with the least cumulative hormone exposure, i.e., earliest gonadectomy.

mcqs.q: A generalised additive model analysis of 20,590 dogs examined cumulative gonadal hormone exposure and cranial cruciate ligament disease (CrCLD) risk. How was this relationship characterised?
mcqs.e: The relationship was nonlinear in both sexes: CrCLD risk was highest with the least cumulative hormone exposure (earliest neuter) and declined sharply to a minimum, confirming a dose-dependent but non-proportional pattern.

mcqs.q: In a study of 20,590 dogs, cranial cruciate ligament disease (CrCLD) risk was nonlinearly associated with cumulative gonadal hormone exposure. At roughly what age did CrCLD risk reach its minimum?
o: ~2.9 years in females and ~2.2 years in males
mcqs.e: CrCLD risk minima were reached at approximately 1054 days (~2.9 yr) in females and 805 days (~2.2 yr) in males, defining these as the thresholds below which early gonadectomy significantly elevates CrCLD risk.

title: Gonadectomy status and age are associated with variable risk of overweight or obese outcomes in 15 dog breeds: a retrospective cohort study using data from primary care veterinary clinics
authors: Valerie A. Benka, John M. Sahrmann, Katherine Rieke, Joyce R. Briggs, Nathaniel Spofford, Stephen Zawistowski, Audrey Ruple, Stefano Romagnoli, Jo Ann Morrison
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
citation: Valerie A. Benka, John M. Sahrmann, Katherine Rieke, Joyce R. Briggs, Nathaniel Spofford, Stephen Zawistowski, Audrey Ruple, Stefano Romagnoli, Jo Ann Morrison. Gonadectomy status and age are associated with variable risk of overweight or obese outcomes in 15 dog breeds: a retrospective cohort study using data from primary care veterinary clinics. Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association. 2025.
abstract: Objective: To examine rates of overweight or obese (OvOb) body condition score, including the association between OvOb and gonadectomy, in 15 dog breeds. Methods: The analysis considered the 5 most recorded large breeds (26,369 dogs) and 10 most recorded toy/small breeds (90,002 dogs) in Banfield Pet Hospital's database from 2013 to 2019. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated associations between OvOb and gonadectomy status, gonadectomy age, sex, and primary breed. Results: There was substantial breed variation in underlying (intact dog) OvOb rates among the 15 breeds. Pugs, Golden Retrievers, and Labrador Retrievers had highest underlying susceptibility to OvOb outcomes. There was some variation in relative OvOb rates among breeds, but breeds differing substantially from size group peers were limited. Among all toy/small breeds, gonadectomy at 3 or 6 months had hazard ratios (relative risks) lower than, or not statistically different from, gonadectomy at 1 year or older. Conclusions: Underlying susceptibility to OvOb varies by breed. Gonadectomy offers significant benefits at individual and population levels. As with many veterinary care decisions, however, there is complexity, and associated OvOb risks are not uniform across breeds.

mcqs.q: In toy/small breeds, how did neutering at 3 or 6 months compare with neutering at 1 year or older for overweight/obese risk?
o: Lower than or not significantly different from later neuter
mcqs.e: Early neuter in small breeds carried hazard ratios no worse than later neuter, supporting pediatric neuter safety.

mcqs.q: What did the study find about underlying obesity susceptibility?
o: Substantial breed variation (Pugs, Goldens, Labs highest)
mcqs.e: Underlying overweight/obese susceptibility varied by breed, highest in Pugs, Goldens, and Labs.

mcqs.q: What was the overall conclusion about gonadectomy?
o: It offers significant individual and population benefits, with breed-tailored weight counseling
mcqs.e: Gonadectomy provides meaningful benefits despite non-uniform, breed-dependent obesity risk.

title: Trends in Intake, Length of Stay and Outcome Data in a Portuguese Animal Shelter Between 2018 and 2024
authors: Rui Jardim, Bruno Colaco, Maria de Lurdes Pinto, Sofia Alves-Pimenta
citation: Rui Jardim, Bruno Colaco, Maria de Lurdes Pinto, Sofia Alves-Pimenta. Trends in Intake, Length of Stay and Outcome Data in a Portuguese Animal Shelter Between 2018 and 2024. Animals (Basel). 2026.
abstract: This seven-year retrospective study analyzed 2291 animals (1132 dogs, 1159 cats) admitted to a Portuguese municipal shelter (CVM Feira) between 2018 and 2024 to identify predictors of live outcomes. Descriptive and regression analyses were performed on 1325 adoptable animals. Adoption occurred for 58.9% of these animals, while 41.1% remained in long-term housing, reflecting growing shelter capacity pressures. Length of Stay (LOS) was the strongest predictor of adoption, with extended stays markedly reducing adoption odds and contributing to overcrowding. For dogs, female sex and owner or animal protection association (APA) surrender increased adoption likelihood. Microchipped animals were 71 times more likely to be returned to their owners, although only a small proportion entered the shelter with identification. The overall Live Release Rate (LRR) was 79.7% and Save Rate (SR) 84.7%, highlighting effective life-saving efforts, while the Population Balance Calculation (PBC) of 75.6% revealed challenges in population flow-through. These findings provide evidence that data-driven strategies, including reducing LOS, enforcing microchipping, and applying species-specific management, are essential to optimize municipal shelter operations and improve animal welfare, with insights applicable to broader European and international contexts.

mcqs.q: A seven-year retrospective study (2018–2024) of 1,325 adoptable animals admitted to a Portuguese municipal shelter identified predictors of live outcomes. What was the single strongest predictor of adoption?
o: Length of stay (longer stay markedly reduced adoption odds)
mcqs.e: Extended length of stay was the strongest predictor: the longer an animal remained in the shelter, the lower its odds of adoption, also contributing to overcrowding.

mcqs.q: How much more likely were microchipped animals to be returned to owners?
mcqs.e: Microchipped animals were 71 times more likely to be reunited with owners.

mcqs.q: Based on a seven-year analysis of a Portuguese municipal shelter (2018–2024), which data-driven strategies were recommended to optimize operations and improve animal welfare?
o: Reduce length of stay and enforce microchipping
Lengthen stays to improve animal well-being
mcqs.e: Cutting length of stay and enforcing microchipping were the principal evidence-based levers recommended to improve population flow-through and return-to-owner rates.

title: Use of Kaplan-Meier and Cox regressions in the distribution of length of stay in animal shelters for pre-specified calendar periods: Definition, computation, and examples of dog length of stay in Orange County California
citation: Michael Loizos Mavrovouniotis. Use of Kaplan-Meier and Cox regressions in the distribution of length of stay in animal shelters for pre-specified calendar periods: Definition, computation, and examples of dog length of stay in Orange County California. PLOS One. 2026.
abstract: Computations of length of stay in animal shelters rely on fixed animal cohorts. This is appropriate for research studies that pre-select cohorts, but it is problematic for operational assessments of animal shelters in fixed calendar periods or for comparisons among periods or shelters. Considering only the length of stay of animals whose stay ended within the study period leads to misinterpretation. The use of the Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards methods with left-truncation and right-censoring is proposed to correctly account for all animals present in the shelter for any fraction of a study period, including those that were present at the beginning and those that remain in care at the end of the period. Examples of dog length of stay in Orange County Animal Care in California show that this computation method corrects the misleading view of historically used calculations of length of stay. Statistically significant changes in length of stay are observed in 8 out of 23 quarterly periods. In a comparison of length of stay before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, the observed significant change in length of stay cannot be explained by variations in sizes and ages of incoming dogs and may be connected to operational policies that restricted visitor access. The proposed approach enables timely tracking of length of stay, accurate comparisons, and assessment of shelter practices and resource needs.

mcqs.q: A methodological study proposed using survival analysis to improve animal shelter length-of-stay (LOS) estimates for fixed calendar periods. Why are conventional LOS calculations biased in this context?
o: They overcount the total number of animals
They include only animals whose stay ended within the period, ignoring animals still in care
They rely on random sampling of records
They are unbiased and always accurate
mcqs.e: Conventional LOS calculations count only completed stays, excluding animals present but not yet discharged, which underestimates true LOS and misrepresents operational performance.

mcqs.q: To correct bias in animal shelter length-of-stay (LOS) estimates during fixed calendar periods, which statistical approach was proposed?
o: Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression with left-truncation and right-censoring
mcqs.e: Survival analysis methods (Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards) with left-truncation and right-censoring correctly account for all animals present during any fraction of the study period, including those not yet discharged.

mcqs.q: A survival-analysis approach to computing animal shelter length of stay (LOS) was applied to dog data from Orange County Animal Care, California, comparing periods before and after the COVID-19 pandemic. What did the corrected analysis reveal?
o: No change in LOS across periods
A genuine post-COVID increase in LOS not explained by changes in dog size or age at intake
LOS decreased after the COVID-19 pandemic
The data were unusable due to the pandemic
mcqs.e: The corrected survival-analysis method revealed a real post-COVID LOS increase that could not be attributed to differences in incoming dog demographics, suggesting it was linked to operational changes such as restricted visitor access.

title: U.S. residents' self-reported access to veterinary care and implications for care-seeking decisions
authors: K. Pasteur, N. O. Widmar, C. V. Tran, C. C. Croney
citation: K. Pasteur, N. O. Widmar, C. V. Tran, C. C. Croney. U.S. residents' self-reported access to veterinary care and implications for care-seeking decisions. Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 2025.
abstract: Introduction: Constrained access to veterinary care may significantly affect the health and welfare of millions of pets nationwide, but little is known about how pet families' experiences with veterinary care or their perceptions of its accessibility and quality may influence their care-seeking decisions. This study examined relationships between pet owners' demographics, perceived access to veterinary care, and related decisions and preferences. Methods: An online survey targeted 1,177 adults who were representative of the U.S. population in terms of sex, age, region, education, and income level. All participants provided their perceptions on 'access to veterinary care'; only pet owners (n = 1,026) were asked about their perceptions of alternative service providers (e.g., veterinary technicians, mid-tier veterinary professionals). Similarly, only care-seekers (n = 236) were asked about their experiences with veterinarians; care-seekers who experienced barriers to care (n = 210) responded to questions regarding their willingness to seek alternative providers. Chi-square tests of independence were used to examine relationships between respondents' demographics, perceived access to care, and preferences for veterinary service providers. Results: Of all survey participants, most defined 'access to care' in terms of service provider availability (78.2%), ease of communication (77.8%), and affordability (74.7%). A majority (54.7%) of care-seekers reported distrusting their veterinarians and 36.8% reported being dissatisfied with their veterinarian's interactions with them despite being satisfied with their pet's care. Many pet owners believed veterinary technicians (66.7%) and mid-tier veterinary professionals (65.1%) could provide quality care equivalent to a veterinarian and preferred to seek care from them rather than forego it. Age, education, and income level were related to pet owners' perceptions of alternative providers and care-seeking decisions. Those under 45, without an advanced degree, or earning under $100,000+ reported higher levels of agreement with statements about alternative providers, indicating more favorable perceptions. Discussion: These findings illustrate how pet owners' experiences while accessing care may influence their perceptions of veterinarians, satisfaction with them, and care-seeking decisions, including their willingness to seek alternative care providers. Further, they reiterate the need for solutions that enhance care-seeker access to high quality veterinary care and promote good animal health and welfare outcomes.

mcqs.q: A US national online survey of 1,177 adults (representative by sex, age, region, education, and income) examined perceptions of access to veterinary care. How did most respondents define 'access to veterinary care'?
o: Provider availability, ease of communication, and affordability
mcqs.e: The top three components cited were service provider availability (78%), ease of communication (78%), and affordability (75%), reflecting a multidimensional definition of access beyond cost alone.

mcqs.q: In a US national survey examining access to veterinary care, 236 participants who had actively sought care for their pets were asked about their experiences with veterinarians. What did over half of these care-seekers report?
mcqs.e: 54.7% of care-seekers reported distrusting their veterinarian, and 36.8% were dissatisfied with the interaction even when satisfied with their pet's care — a finding with significant implications for the veterinary–client relationship.

mcqs.q: A US national survey of pet owners found that most (about two-thirds) believed veterinary technicians and mid-tier veterinary professionals could provide quality care equivalent to a veterinarian, and preferred them over forgoing care entirely. Which care-delivery model do these findings support?
o: Expanded roles for veterinary technicians and mid-tier providers (spectrum-of-care model)
Mandatory specialist referral for all cases
