mcqs.e: Most pet owners would accept technicians or mid-tier professionals rather than forgo care, and those under 45, without advanced degrees, or earning less reported more favorable perceptions — supporting expanded-role, spectrum-of-care models.

title: Utilizing the Human Animal Bond to Promote Preventive Care Engagement in Underserved Communities: A Descriptive Study of 2 U.S. One Health Clinics
authors: Aguirre Siliezar K, Patel S, Chande R, Joiner A, Hoover MC, Mathis MW, Hendrickson J, Siliezar J, Jankowski K
journal: Journal of Primary Care & Community Health
citation: Aguirre Siliezar K, Patel S, Chande R, Joiner A, Hoover MC, Mathis MW, Hendrickson J, Siliezar J, Jankowski K. Utilizing the Human Animal Bond to Promote Preventive Care Engagement in Underserved Communities: A Descriptive Study of 2 U.S. One Health Clinics. Journal of Primary Care & Community Health. 2025.
abstract: The purpose of this descriptive study was to strengthen understanding of the human-animal bond and the impact of One Health Clinics (OHCs) on the communities they serve. We aimed to assess how joint access to veterinary care and human health services enables community members to engage with healthcare for themselves. Individuals attending 2 OHCs in the United States were surveyed to gain insight into reasons for attending OHCs, attitudes on the human-animal bond, healthcare access and utilization, and pet owner satisfaction and trust toward medical and veterinary professionals. Both clinics operated in areas with limited medical and veterinary healthcare access, but varied in clinic structure and availability of human healthcare volunteers. A total of 175 surveys were analyzed. Most participants attended primarily for veterinary services (Clinic A: 91%, Clinic B: 75%). However, a significantly higher proportion of Clinic B participants received health screenings (91% vs 32%, P < .0001), learned new health information (48% vs 31%, P = .0129), and were provided with follow-up health resources (84% vs 51%, P = .000007). Across both sites, the majority expressed high trust in medical and veterinary providers (Clinic A: 84%-95%, Clinic B: 90%-98%) and reported high satisfaction with the care received. Most participants considered their pets vital family members (Clinic A: 81%, Clinic B: 93%), and many credited their pets with supporting physical activity and reducing feelings of depression and loneliness. Importantly, a majority of respondents at both clinics indicated they were more likely to seek healthcare for themselves if veterinary services were also available (Clinic A: 56%, Clinic B: 72%). These findings suggest that OHCs have the potential to enhance access to human healthcare in underserved communities by utilizing veterinary services as a point of engagement. Participants reported a strong bond with their pet. Based on reported levels of trust and satisfaction, the OHC model may help strengthen relationships between underserved communities and human healthcare and veterinary professionals.

mcqs.q: What was the primary reason most participants attended the two One Health Clinics?
mcqs.e: Most attendees came primarily for veterinary services (Clinic A 91%, Clinic B 75%).

mcqs.q: A descriptive study surveyed 175 attendees at two US One Health Clinics serving underserved communities, where veterinary and human health services were co-located. What did a majority of respondents report about their own health-seeking behavior?
o: They avoided human healthcare due to cost
They preferred human-only clinics over co-located models
They were more likely to seek healthcare for themselves when veterinary services were also available
They trusted veterinarians less than physicians
mcqs.e: A majority at both clinics (Clinic A: 56%, Clinic B: 72%) said co-located veterinary services made them more likely to seek healthcare for themselves, demonstrating the leverage of the human-animal bond in underserved communities.

mcqs.q: The study concluded that co-located One Health Clinics can primarily serve as a tool to do what?
o: Enhance human healthcare access in underserved communities via veterinary engagement
mcqs.e: Authors concluded OHCs leverage the human-animal bond to boost human healthcare engagement in underserved communities.

title: One health and human animal-bond intervention strategies- assessing veterinary-social service collaborations
authors: Orchard RJ, Scarbrough E, Crow A, Baldwin M, Moreau C
citation: Orchard RJ, Scarbrough E, Crow A, Baldwin M, Moreau C. One health and human animal-bond intervention strategies- assessing veterinary-social service collaborations. Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 2026.
abstract: This study evaluates a novel interdisciplinary outreach model integrating veterinary care, social work, and public health services to serve unhoused populations and their companion animals in Topeka, Kansas. Grounded in structural vulnerability theory and One Health principles, the project examined the Street Dog Coalition's (SDC) partnership with the Mobile Access Partnership (MAP), focusing on how the human-animal bond functions as a catalyst for trust, engagement, and care continuity. Using a qualitatively driven, mixed-methods design, the research team conducted 12 semi-structured interviews with beneficiaries, volunteers, program staff, and external collaborators, supplemented by descriptive service utilization data. Thematic analysis revealed six interrelated themes: the transformative power of the human-animal bond, trust-building as foundational to engagement, structural barriers to care continuity, tensions in the graduation process, emotional impact on providers, and the emergence of a relational ecosystem of care. Findings underscore the relational and structural dynamics of service delivery, highlighting the dual importance of compassionate, trauma-informed care and policy-level reforms. This research contributes to the growing evidence base for integrated One Health interventions and offers critical insight into how veterinary-social service collaborations can operationalize equity, dignity, and mutual healing in structurally vulnerable contexts.

mcqs.q: In this veterinary-social service outreach model for unhoused people, the human-animal bond functioned mainly as what?
o: A catalyst for trust, engagement, and care continuity
mcqs.e: Thematic analysis framed the human-animal bond as a catalyst for trust, engagement, and care continuity.

mcqs.q: A mixed-methods study evaluated a veterinary-social service collaboration serving unhoused people and their companion animals in Topeka, Kansas, finding that the human-animal bond was key to trust and engagement. Beyond compassionate clinical care, what did the study emphasize was needed for sustained success?
o: Mandatory vaccination laws for companion animals
More veterinary specialists in the collaboration
Trauma-informed service delivery plus policy-level reform to address structural barriers
Higher service fees to ensure program sustainability
mcqs.e: Thematic analysis highlighted that trauma-informed care must be paired with policy reform addressing structural barriers to care continuity — clinical compassion alone is insufficient for lasting impact on structurally vulnerable populations.

title: Assessing client needs in community veterinary care: a case study from WisCARES
authors: Schultz K, Alvarez E, Brooks J, Chun R
citation: Schultz K, Alvarez E, Brooks J, Chun R. Assessing client needs in community veterinary care: a case study from WisCARES. Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 2025.
abstract: As community veterinary clinics expand across the United States, there is a growing recognition that services need to be aligned with the specific needs of clients and their companion animals, which may vary from one community to the next. WisCARES Community Clinic, which has served low-income pet owners in Dane County, Wisconsin for over a decade, conducted a comprehensive needs assessment in the summer of 2024 to re-evaluate the support required by its clientele. Through an interviewer-administered survey of 51 clients, conducted either in person or by phone, the study identified key areas for assistance. Clients most frequently reported needing support with pet food, treats, pet cleaning supplies, and dental care items, as well as access to affordable grooming services. In addition, many clients expressed a need for help navigating social services and securing reliable transportation. These findings highlight that clients experiencing poverty require more than basic veterinary care to maintain the health and well-being of their pets. While local contexts vary, this assessment offers valuable insight for other community veterinary programs seeking to allocate limited resources to where they will have the greatest impact.

mcqs.q: What did the WisCARES needs assessment find low-income clients most frequently needed?
o: Pet food, supplies, dental/grooming items, and transportation
mcqs.e: Top reported needs were pet food, supplies, dental and grooming items, grooming access, transportation, and social-service navigation.

mcqs.q: A 2024 needs assessment of 51 low-income pet owners served by the WisCARES Community Clinic in Dane County, Wisconsin reached which central conclusion about clients experiencing poverty?
o: They need more than basic veterinary care — wraparound support
mcqs.e: The WisCARES assessment found poverty-affected owners require wraparound support beyond clinical care — including pet food, supplies, grooming, transportation, and social-service navigation — and that local contexts vary, so resources should be allocated to where they will have the greatest impact.

title: Veterinary clinicians as One Health messengers: opportunities for preventing zoonoses while promoting biophilia in the United States
citation: Overcast M. Veterinary clinicians as One Health messengers: opportunities for preventing zoonoses while promoting biophilia in the United States. Frontiers in Conservation Science. 2025.
abstract: One Health is a transdisciplinary approach to health science that recognizes the linked and interdependent ecology of environmental, human, and animal health. Effective communication of zoonotic disease risks through a One Health framework presents an opportunity to both prevent emerging infectious diseases and enhance public appreciation for wildlife and conservation, herein termed biophilia. While veterinary practitioners have historically played a pivotal role in public health and conservation, structural changes in the veterinary profession—including the dominance of companion animal practice, fee-for-service models, and corporate consolidation—limit their potential as One Health communicators, and thus wildlife conservation advocates. Additionally, the human-animal bond is often singularly framed as a health resource for pet owners and companion animals, neglecting its broader role within communities and its connection to other social, ecological, and epidemiological networks that include human and wildlife populations. This article outlines key constraints facing veterinarians as One Health communicators and proposes two solutions to integrate preventive zoonoses messaging and biophilia promotion within veterinary clinical practice: (1) the human-animal bond should be reconceptualized within veterinary clinical sciences as a community-level resource akin to natural capital, and (2) the veterinary extension workforce should be expanded to include agents facilitating local conservation and public health information exchange with companion animal veterinarians. Through these solutions, the veterinary profession can further enhance its principal role in One Health. Such efforts would empower veterinarians to communicate about zoonotic disease risks and conservation, ensuring that One Health principles are embedded in everyday clinical interactions and broader community initiatives.

mcqs.q: A commentary arguing that veterinary clinicians should serve as One Health messengers for zoonosis prevention identified which structural changes in the veterinary profession as key constraints on that role?
o: Companion-animal dominance, fee-for-service models, and corporate consolidation
mcqs.e: The article cites the dominance of companion-animal practice, fee-for-service models, and corporate consolidation as structural factors that limit veterinarians' capacity to act as One Health communicators and wildlife conservation advocates.

mcqs.q: A 2025 article on veterinary clinicians as One Health messengers proposed reconceptualizing the human-animal bond in what way to broaden its public-health relevance?
o: As a community-level resource akin to natural capital
mcqs.e: The article argues the human-animal bond should be reframed as a community-level resource comparable to natural capital, connecting pet ownership to broader social, ecological, and epidemiological networks rather than treating it as a purely private benefit.

title: The One Health Clinic: Care for Young Adults and Companion Animals Experiencing Homelessness
authors: Rejto N, Ramirez V, Fenelon HT, Xie M, Kuehl K, Terry A, Tin AH, Tabor E, Schneier K, Nee A, Richer A, Rabinowitz P, Meisner J
journal: Journal of Primary Care & Community Health
citation: Rejto N, Ramirez V, Fenelon HT, Xie M, Kuehl K, Terry A, Tin AH, Tabor E, Schneier K, Nee A, Richer A, Rabinowitz P, Meisner J. The One Health Clinic: Care for Young Adults and Companion Animals Experiencing Homelessness. Journal of Primary Care & Community Health. 2025.
abstract: Introduction/Objective: This study evaluates 4 years of data from the Seattle One Health Clinic (OHC), a novel model for clinical care which integrates human and animal health care services for youth and young adults experiencing homelessness (YPEH) and their pets. Methods: We analyzed deidentified data from standardized OHC visit forms, electronic medical records, and veterinary records from 2019 to 2022. We assessed the overlaps between human and animal healthcare provided and the impact of environmental stressors on both human and animal patients. Results: Over 50% of all human clients established healthcare for the first time in 2 years, with 85% attending one or more follow-up appointments with non-emergency healthcare services within 2 years following their initial OHC appointment. All animals received care during their visit. Needs addressed at the human-animal interface included zoonotic infections, animal allergies, and mental/behavioral health. The most common client-pet reported environmental concerns were food insecurity, heat, and cold. Conclusion: Our results suggest integrated human and animal healthcare is a feasible and acceptable model of care for YPEH to access acute and preventative care at the human-animal-environmental interface. This approach holds promise for increasing health-seeking behaviors, and engagement in preventative, therapeutic, and follow-up care.

mcqs.q: What did over half of human clients at the Seattle One Health Clinic do?
o: Established healthcare for the first time in 2 years
mcqs.e: Over 50% established healthcare for the first time in 2 years.

mcqs.q: In a 4-year evaluation (2019–2022) of the Seattle One Health Clinic—which integrated human and veterinary healthcare for youth experiencing homelessness and their pets—what proportion of human clients attended one or more non-emergency follow-up appointments within 2 years of their initial visit?
mcqs.e: 85% of clients at the Seattle One Health Clinic attended at least one non-emergency follow-up appointment within 2 years of their initial visit, demonstrating strong engagement with preventive care.

mcqs.q: A study evaluating 4 years of data (2019–2022) from the Seattle One Health Clinic—integrating human and veterinary care for youth experiencing homelessness—concluded that this integrated model was:
o: A feasible, acceptable model that promotes health-seeking
mcqs.e: Authors concluded integrated human and animal healthcare is a feasible and acceptable model for youth experiencing homelessness, promising for increasing health-seeking behaviors across acute, preventive, therapeutic, and follow-up care.

title: Global Perspectives on Rabies Control and Elimination: A Scoping Review of Dog Owners' Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices
authors: Das M, Yustyniuk V, Perez AM, Perez Aguirreburualde MS
citation: Das M, Yustyniuk V, Perez AM, Perez Aguirreburualde MS. Global Perspectives on Rabies Control and Elimination: A Scoping Review of Dog Owners' Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices. Pathogens. 2025.
abstract: Rabies is a fatal but entirely vaccine-preventable disease, with the highest risk in areas where free-roaming domestic dogs are prevalent. Understanding dog owners' knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) is crucial for shaping effective rabies control strategies. This scoping review aimed to synthesize global evidence from studies evaluating dog owners' KAP to identify behavioral factors relevant to rabies prevention and control. A systematic literature search was conducted using PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus, covering the period from 2012 to 2025. Seventy full-text articles were included based on predefined criteria. The findings reveal substantial gaps in dog owners' knowledge, beliefs, and behaviors regarding rabies prevention. While general awareness of rabies is high among dog owners, their knowledge about transmission, clinical signs, and the fatal nature of the disease is inconsistent, with significant variability across studies. The vaccination uptake also varied widely across studies, ranging from less than 1% to over 90%, with no study reporting full coverage. Furthermore, a strong positive correlation was found between vaccination practice and the awareness of vaccine benefits (r = 0.69, p = 0.004). Common barriers to vaccination include lack of information, vaccine accessibility, distance to clinics, and personal constraints. These insights underscore the importance of early and targeted communication about vaccination campaigns. Future research should focus on periodically evaluating KAP before and after interventions to better inform rabies control efforts.

mcqs.q: Across the 70 included studies, dog rabies-vaccination uptake ranged how widely?
o: From less than 1% to over 90%, with none reaching full coverage
mcqs.e: Uptake ranged from <1% to >90% with no study reporting full coverage.

mcqs.q: In a 2025 global scoping review of dog owners' knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding rabies prevention (70 studies, 2012–2025), which factor showed a strong positive correlation (r = 0.69, p = 0.004) with vaccination practice?
mcqs.e: Across studies included in this KAP scoping review, owner awareness of vaccine benefits correlated strongly (r = 0.69, p = 0.004) with vaccination practice, underscoring targeted communication as a key lever for improving coverage.

mcqs.q: A 2025 global scoping review of dog owner knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) for rabies control (70 studies, 2012–2025) identified which common barriers to dog vaccination?
o: Lack of information, vaccine accessibility, and distance to clinics
mcqs.e: The scoping review identified lack of information, vaccine accessibility, distance to clinics, and personal constraints as the common barriers to vaccination across the included studies.

title: A unique approach to fostering student wellbeing while supporting community needs through an interprofessional, One Health, access to care veterinary clinic: WisCARES
authors: Alvarez EE, Chun R, Brooks JW, Schultz K, Lygo-Baker S
citation: Alvarez EE, Chun R, Brooks JW, Schultz K, Lygo-Baker S. A unique approach to fostering student wellbeing while supporting community needs through an interprofessional, One Health, access to care veterinary clinic: WisCARES. Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 2025.
abstract: Service-learning integrating student education into academically relevant service activities addressing community needs enables students to learn and practice multiple skills. WisCARES (Wisconsin Companion Animal Resources, Education and Social Services) represents a service-learning clinic where veterinarians, veterinary nurses, and social workers collaborate as an interprofessional team within a One Health access-to-care setting serving both veterinary patients and their human companions. Beyond hands-on spectrum of care experiences, veterinary students gain insight into poverty, homelessness, and social determinants of health, understanding how these factors influence client decision-making and treatment adherence. Students additionally work with social workers exploring how moral stress and perfectionism affect personal physical and mental health, developing individualized self-care strategies. WisCARES aims to develop veterinarians who become positive profession contributors by identifying and addressing personal biases while deliberately incorporating access-to-care medicine into their future practice, benefiting both their veterinary teams and their served communities.

mcqs.q: Beyond clinical skills, what did WisCARES students gain insight into?
o: Poverty, homelessness, and social determinants of health
mcqs.e: Students gained insight into poverty, homelessness, and social determinants influencing client decisions.

mcqs.q: At WisCARES—an interprofessional, One Health, access-to-care service-learning clinic in Wisconsin serving low-income pet owners—which team members collaborated to provide care?
o: Veterinarians, veterinary nurses, and social workers
mcqs.e: The WisCARES One Health team comprised veterinarians, veterinary nurses, and social workers operating as an interprofessional unit to address both veterinary and human social-service needs.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance in European Companion Animals Practice: A One Health Approach
authors: Monteiro HIG, Silva V, de Sousa T, Calouro R, Saraiva S, Igrejas G, Poeta P
citation: Monteiro HIG, Silva V, de Sousa T, Calouro R, Saraiva S, Igrejas G, Poeta P. Antimicrobial Resistance in European Companion Animals Practice: A One Health Approach. Animals (Basel). 2025.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global health emergency. The growing levels of multidrug-resistant bacteria in companion animals represent a critical but under-recognized threat, as pets can act as reservoirs and vectors of resistant pathogens, and bacteria can spread between species. Despite living in close proximity to humans and sharing many of the same antibiotic classes, companion animals remain largely overlooked in the AMR control strategies. A major obstacle to combating AMR in Europe is the absence of a mandatory and uniform surveillance system. Without a standardized approach, data collection remains inconsistent, leading to knowledge gaps and hindering effective investigation and policymaking. Surveillance failures prevent a comprehensive understanding of resistance patterns, making it difficult to implement timely and evidence-based measures. Existing laws and regulations are insufficient to contain the growing threat of AMR. Current policies fail to enforce strict antimicrobial stewardship across all European countries and lack the necessary scope to address resistance effectively. Urgent action is required—Europe must implement stronger, harmonized surveillance systems, enforce stricter veterinary antimicrobial regulations, and develop more active and binding programs to curb resistance before it reaches an uncontrollable level. A One Health approach, recognizing the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health, is essential.

mcqs.q: What role do companion animals play in antimicrobial resistance, per this review?
o: They are immune to resistant bacteria
They are reservoirs and vectors of multidrug-resistant bacteria that can spread to humans
mcqs.e: Pets act as under-recognized reservoirs and vectors of resistant pathogens shared with humans.

mcqs.q: A 2025 One Health review of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in European companion animal practice identified which structural obstacle as the major barrier to combating AMR across Europe?
o: Absence of a mandatory, uniform surveillance system
mcqs.e: The review identified the lack of a mandatory, harmonised surveillance system across Europe as the key barrier, resulting in inconsistent data, knowledge gaps, and ineffective policymaking on companion-animal AMR.

mcqs.q: Which overarching framework did the paper deem essential for AMR control?
mcqs.e: A One Health approach linking human, animal, and environmental health was deemed essential.

title: Chasing rabies herd immunity: evaluating dog vaccination strategies and post-vaccination survey reliability in urban and peri-urban Bangladesh
authors: Swedberg C, Siddiqi UR, Keshavamurthy R, Rana MS, Islam K, Kennedy E, Ross YB, Bonaparte S, Lohr F, Mursalin HS, Kamruzzaman M, Gamble L, Gibson AD, Blanton JD, Wallace RM
citation: Swedberg C, Siddiqi UR, Keshavamurthy R, Rana MS, Islam K, Kennedy E, Ross YB, Bonaparte S, Lohr F, Mursalin HS, Kamruzzaman M, Gamble L, Gibson AD, Blanton JD, Wallace RM. Chasing rabies herd immunity: evaluating dog vaccination strategies and post-vaccination survey reliability in urban and peri-urban Bangladesh. Frontiers in Microbiology. 2026.
abstract: Mass dog vaccination (MDV) is essential for eliminating dog-mediated rabies, responsible for over 95% of the estimated 74,000 annual human rabies deaths. Achieving ≥ 70% vaccination coverage necessary for herd immunity remains challenging, underscoring the need for effective vaccination strategies and reliable post-vaccination evaluation methods. MDV campaigns were conducted in four site in Bangladesh (two urban, two peri-urban) using three strategies: standard capture-vaccinate-release (CVR), enhanced CVR (eCVR), and roaming static point (RSP). Post-vaccination sight re-sight (SRS) and household surveys were used to characterize dog populations and estimate coverage. Three enumeration methods were compared to assess reliability and utility for campaign evaluation. Over 12 working days, 9,195 dogs were vaccinated. eCVR achieved the highest operational efficiency (40.2 dogs/vaccinator/day), followed by standard CVR (36.6) and RSP (18.2). Post-vaccination surveys indicated that over 93% of dogs were free-roaming, and around 30% were unowned, highlighting limitations of static point strategies. Human-to-dog ratios (HDRs) were lower than the 100:1 planning estimate and varied widely across sites (mean: 67.8; range: 21.1–129.6), with no significant difference between urban and peri-urban areas (p = 0.479). Coverage estimates differed by enumeration method: 19% (dog density), 32% (HDR), and 47% (SRS), with comparable SRS- and HDR-based estimates (p = 0.920), and dog density formula estimates significantly lower (p = 0.014). Averaging across enumeration methods and sites, eCVR achieved the highest coverage (45%), followed by standard CVR (37%) and RSP (16%), with estimated RSP coverage significantly lower than eCVR (p = 0.028). The wide heterogeneity in HDRs highlights the limitations of using a single ratio for national dog population extrapolation. Effective rabies control requires locally tailored vaccination strategies, real-time monitoring, and robust enumeration techniques to guide planning and ensure reliable evaluation of campaign impact.

mcqs.q: What vaccination coverage threshold is needed for dog-mediated rabies herd immunity?
mcqs.e: Herd immunity for dog-mediated rabies requires ≥70% coverage.

mcqs.q: A study evaluating mass dog rabies vaccination in urban and peri-urban Bangladesh compared three delivery strategies—standard capture-vaccinate-release (CVR), enhanced CVR (eCVR), and roaming static point (RSP). Which strategy achieved the highest operational efficiency and vaccination coverage?
mcqs.e: eCVR achieved the highest operational efficiency (40.2 dogs/vaccinator/day) and the highest average vaccination coverage (45%) across enumeration methods and sites in the Bangladesh study.

mcqs.q: In a Bangladesh mass dog rabies vaccination study comparing capture-vaccinate-release and static-point delivery strategies, what did post-vaccination surveys reveal about the dog population that limited the effectiveness of static-point methods?
mcqs.e: More than 93% of dogs were free-roaming and approximately 30% were unowned, meaning fixed static-point sites could not effectively reach most of the target population.

title: Animal rabies prevention and control in Shanghai, China: policies and practices, 2011–2025
authors: Zhu T, Chang X, Wu X, Xia L, Zhu X, Zhu J, Li Z, Chen W, Fan Y, Tang Y, Liu J, Zhao H
citation: Zhu T, Chang X, Wu X, Xia L, Zhu X, Zhu J, Li Z, Chen W, Fan Y, Tang Y, Liu J, Zhao H. Animal rabies prevention and control in Shanghai, China: policies and practices, 2011–2025. Frontiers in Public Health. 2026.
abstract: Background: Rabies remains a public health issue in Shanghai, with human cases reported since 2006, necessitating sustained multi-faceted control. Strategies: Key measures include mandatory canine vaccination, increased access to vaccination services (19–431 by 2025), management of free-roaming animals, and public education campaigns. Challenges and perspective: Challenges persist—particularly the low vaccination coverage among free-roaming animals. Future priorities involve developing oral rabies vaccines for free-roaming animals, enhancing wildlife rabies surveillance, expanding insurance coverage for postexposure prophylaxis, and strengthening cross-sector collaboration through the One Health framework. Conclusion: Shanghai's integrated strategies have reduced human rabies. Achieving the 2030 zero-death goal requires closing gaps in free-roaming animal vaccination and postexposure prophylaxis access.

mcqs.q: What persistent challenge did Shanghai's rabies program identify?
o: Low vaccination coverage among free-roaming animals
mcqs.e: The residual gap was low vaccination coverage in free-roaming/unowned animals.

mcqs.q: A 2026 review of Shanghai's animal rabies prevention and control policies and practices (2011–2025) named which novel tool as a future priority for closing the vaccination gap among free-roaming animals?
mcqs.e: Developing oral rabies vaccines for free-roaming animals was identified as a priority because conventional injectable vaccination cannot easily reach unowned and stray animals.

title: Prevalence, risk factors, and zoonotic implications of gastrointestinal parasites in urban cats in Kazakhstan: A cross-sectional multicity study
authors: Lider LA, Kiyan V, Seitkamzina DM, Ussenbayev A, Akmambaeva BE, Uakhit RS, Mannapova NE, Sytnik I, Bauer C
citation: Lider LA, Kiyan V, Seitkamzina DM, Ussenbayev A, Akmambaeva BE, Uakhit RS, Mannapova NE, Sytnik I, Bauer C. Prevalence, risk factors, and zoonotic implications of gastrointestinal parasites in urban cats in Kazakhstan: A cross-sectional multicity study. Veterinary World. 2025.
abstract: Cats act as reservoirs for various gastrointestinal parasites, including species of significant zoonotic concern such as Toxocara cati, Toxoplasma gondii, and Giardia intestinalis. However, data on the prevalence and risk factors associated with feline endoparasites in Kazakhstan remain limited. This study aimed to determine the prevalence, species diversity, and risk factors of intestinal parasitic infections in urban cat populations across five major cities in Kazakhstan, thereby supporting the One Health framework for the prevention of zoonotic diseases. A cross-sectional survey was conducted from August 2023 to January 2025, involving 1,301 fecal samples collected from both client-owned and stray cats in Almaty, Astana, Oral, Qostanai, and Shymkent. Standardized Sheather's sugar flotation was used to detect helminth eggs and coccidia oocysts in all samples, while Giardia coproantigen was assessed in 1,256 samples using a commercial immunochromatographic assay (FASTest CRYPTO-GIARDIA strip test kit, MEGACOR, Austria). Prevalence differences across categories – ownership status, sex, age class, and city – were evaluated using the Chi-squared test, and odds ratios (OR) were calculated to identify significant risk factors. Overall, 17.7% (230/1,301) of cats were infected with at least one intestinal parasite species. The most prevalent species were Cystoisospora felis (7.2%), T. cati (6.2%), Cystoisospora rivolta (2.0%), and Giardia (6.4%). T. gondii-like oocysts (T. gondii or Hammondia hammondi) were detected in 0.6% of samples. Significant variation in parasite prevalence was observed among cities. Stray cats were significantly more likely to harbor C. felis and C. rivolta. Female cats had higher odds of testing positive for Giardia (OR = 1.8). Infections with T. cati, C. felis, and Giardia showed a significant association with age, with kittens (<6 months) being approximately twice as likely to test positive for these parasites compared to adult cats. This study represents the first comprehensive assessment of gastrointestinal parasitism in urban cats in Kazakhstan. The detection of zoonotic parasites and identification of significant demographic risk factors underscore the need for enhanced public health strategies, including educational outreach, targeted deworming protocols, and environmental hygiene measures. Future molecular investigations are necessary to differentiate T. gondii from Hammondia hammondi and to genotype Giardia assemblages. Soil surveillance in public spaces is also recommended to assess environmental contamination and potential exposure risk to humans, particularly children.

mcqs.q: In a 2023–2025 cross-sectional study testing 1,301 fecal samples from urban cats across five cities in Kazakhstan, what proportion was infected with at least one gastrointestinal (GI) parasite?
mcqs.e: 230 of 1,301 cats (17.7%) carried at least one intestinal parasite species, with Cystoisospora felis (7.2%), Toxocara cati (6.2%), and Giardia (6.4%) as the most prevalent.

mcqs.q: In a cross-sectional study of gastrointestinal parasites in urban cats across five cities in Kazakhstan (n = 1,301), which age group had approximately double the odds of testing positive for Toxocara cati, Cystoisospora felis, and Giardia compared with adult cats?
mcqs.e: Kittens under 6 months were approximately twice as likely to test positive for T. cati, C. felis, and Giardia compared with adult cats in this Kazakhstan urban cat study.

mcqs.q: In a multicity cross-sectional study of gastrointestinal parasites in urban cats in Kazakhstan (1,256 samples tested for coproantigen), female cats had significantly higher odds (OR = 1.8) of testing positive for which parasite compared with male cats?
mcqs.e: Female sex was independently associated with higher Giardia positivity (OR = 1.8) in this Kazakhstan urban cat parasite study.

title: Evaluating delivery models for mass dog vaccination: a cost-effectiveness analysis of community-led and team-led vaccination strategies for rabies control in resource-limited settings
authors: Changalucha J, Anderson D, Yoder J, Stone B, Lugelo A, Kimera S, Lupindu A, Hampson K, Lankester F
citation: Changalucha J, Anderson D, Yoder J, Stone B, Lugelo A, Kimera S, Lupindu A, Hampson K, Lankester F. Evaluating delivery models for mass dog vaccination: a cost-effectiveness analysis of community-led and team-led vaccination strategies for rabies control in resource-limited settings. Frontiers in Tropical Diseases. 2026.
abstract: Mass dog vaccination (MDV) against rabies is a cost-effective intervention to eliminate rabies in humans. Although all mammals can transmit the virus, domestic dogs remain the main vectors of transmission to humans and a range of other species. Effective MDV delivery has the potential to prevent approximately 60,000 human deaths every year in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC), where rabies is endemic in domestic dog populations. Although widely recognised as the most cost-effective intervention for rabies control, MDV remains underfunded and underused in many rabies-endemic countries; governments often prioritise investment in human post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), which, although life-saving, is more expensive and does not address the source of infection. One major barrier to the widespread adoption of MDV is weak public delivery infrastructure in many LMICs, contributing to high operational costs and logistical complexity. This study evaluated cost-effectiveness by comparing a community-led hybrid vaccination strategy against the standard team-led approach in northern Tanzania, measuring economic metrics from provider and societal perspectives. The community-led strategy had higher annual ward-level costs (approximately $1,729) than the team-led approach (approximately $884) but vaccinated roughly twice as many dogs (768 vs 350); cost per dog vaccinated was comparable between approaches, with team-led cheaper in urban settings and community-led more efficient in rural areas. The authors conclude that both delivery strategies are viable to increase dog rabies vaccination, but their cost-effectiveness is context-specific, recommending community-led approaches for rural expansion and team-led methods for densely populated urban environments.

mcqs.q: Why is mass dog vaccination considered more strategically valuable than human post-exposure prophylaxis?
o: It is always cheaper per person
It addresses the source of infection
mcqs.e: Unlike PEP, MDV targets the source of transmission, making it the most cost-effective control.

mcqs.q: In a cost-effectiveness analysis comparing community-led and team-led mass dog rabies vaccination strategies in northern Tanzania, which delivery approach was more cost-efficient in rural settings?
mcqs.e: Community-led delivery vaccinated roughly twice as many dogs as team-led at a comparable per-dog cost and was specifically more efficient in rural areas of northern Tanzania.

mcqs.q: A cost-effectiveness analysis of community-led versus team-led mass dog rabies vaccination in northern Tanzania concluded that the optimal choice between strategies was:
mcqs.e: Both delivery models are viable for increasing dog vaccination, but which is optimal depends on context: community-led for rural expansion, team-led for densely populated urban settings.

title: Veterinary Forensic Pathology in the Investigation of Animal Cruelty: Post-Mortem Insights, Forensic Tools, Case Studies, and Legal Perspectives
authors: Julia Francesca Gilbert, Julia Eylül Aysu, István Tóth, Anna Szilasi, Míra Mándoki
citation: Julia Francesca Gilbert, Julia Eylül Aysu, István Tóth, Anna Szilasi, Míra Mándoki. Veterinary Forensic Pathology in the Investigation of Animal Cruelty: Post-Mortem Insights, Forensic Tools, Case Studies, and Legal Perspectives. Animals (MDPI). 2026.
abstract: Veterinary forensic pathology is an evolving discipline at the intersection of veterinary medicine, forensic science, and animal welfare law. This article underscores the growing importance of this field in advancing both animal welfare and justice. Drawing on post-mortem examinations, advanced forensic techniques, and real-world case studies, the article highlights how forensic veterinarians differentiate between ante- and post-mortem injuries, estimate time of death, and interpret complex trauma patterns. It also reviews the application of imaging technologies, bloodstain pattern analysis, forensic entomology, and histological tools in forensic investigations. Through illustrative case examples, including neglect, sexual abuse, thermal injuries, firearm wounds, and asphyxia, the article demonstrates the evidentiary value of veterinary pathology in legal contexts. Finally, the article outlines future directions for the field, emphasizing the need for standardized training, interdisciplinary collaboration, and greater legal recognition.

mcqs.q: Per this review, the core role of the forensic veterinarian in cruelty cases is to:
mcqs.e: The review frames the forensic veterinarian's central function as objective, legally defensible documentation of findings.

mcqs.q: Which capability does forensic necropsy provide according to the article?
mcqs.e: The review highlights differentiating ante- from post-mortem injury, estimating time of death, and interpreting trauma patterns.

mcqs.q: A 2026 review of veterinary forensic pathology in animal cruelty investigations identified which recurring system-level gaps as the field's main needs for advancement?
o: Standardized training and interdisciplinary collaboration/chain of custody
mcqs.e: The review highlights the need for standardized training, interdisciplinary collaboration, and greater legal recognition as the principal gaps limiting veterinary forensic pathology's impact in cruelty cases.

title: Development of an Operational Protocol for Animal Hoarding: A Conceptual Proposal Based on Multidisciplinary Field Experience
authors: Francesca Bellini, Alberto Cal, Alessia Liverini, Gianna Regoli, Giancarlo Ruffo
citation: Francesca Bellini, Alberto Cal, Alessia Liverini, Gianna Regoli, Giancarlo Ruffo. Development of an Operational Protocol for Animal Hoarding: A Conceptual Proposal Based on Multidisciplinary Field Experience. Animals (MDPI). 2025.
abstract: Animal hoarding constitutes a multifaceted challenge impacting animal welfare, public health, and environmental safety. Though recognized clinically as a manifestation of Hoarding Disorder per DSM-5 criteria, structured intervention frameworks remain scarce. Drawing from critical analysis of existing assessment instruments applied across 48 documented cases managed by Italian health authorities (2019-2024), we identified substantial gaps in current tools-particularly regarding psychological dimensions, relational dynamics, and longitudinal monitoring. In response, we present an integrated operational framework comprising three complementary instruments: a preliminary observational screening form, a clinical-relational interview, and a standardized veterinary assessment tool. Structured across four sequential phases-reporting, on-site inspection, case management, and monitoring-the protocol operationalizes multidisciplinary collaboration among veterinarians, mental health professionals, social workers, and law enforcement. Designed with modularity and adaptability for diverse contexts, this conceptual model promotes systematic data collection while recognizing interconnections between animal suffering, human psychological distress, and environmental degradation through a One Welfare lens. Pending experimental validation, the framework provides operational guidance for structured interventions and evidence-gathering supporting research and public health initiatives.

mcqs.q: Animal hoarding is clinically classified as:
o: A manifestation of DSM-5 Hoarding Disorder
mcqs.e: The article recognizes hoarding as a manifestation of Hoarding Disorder per DSM-5 criteria.

mcqs.q: A multidisciplinary operational framework for animal hoarding interventions, developed from analysis of 48 cases managed by Italian health authorities (2019–2024), emphasizes which key intervention beyond the initial removal of animals?
mcqs.e: Because animal hoarding is recognized under DSM-5 Hoarding Disorder and involves psychological dimensions and relational dynamics, the framework emphasises longitudinal monitoring and mental-health professional involvement as essential complements to animal removal.

mcqs.q: A conceptual operational protocol for animal hoarding interventions, developed from Italian field experience with 48 documented cases, is structured across which four sequential phases?
mcqs.e: The operational protocol is organized into four sequential phases: reporting, on-site inspection, case management, and monitoring, enabling systematic data collection and longitudinal intervention across multidisciplinary teams.

title: Evolution of Suspected Cat Abuse Between 2020 and 2024 in the Community of Madrid (Spain)
authors: Nicolás Aradilla, Javier María De Pablo-Moreno, Néstor Porras, Blanca Chinchilla, Antonio Rodríguez-Bertos
citation: Nicolás Aradilla, Javier María De Pablo-Moreno, Néstor Porras, Blanca Chinchilla, Antonio Rodríguez-Bertos. Evolution of Suspected Cat Abuse Between 2020 and 2024 in the Community of Madrid (Spain). Animals (MDPI). 2025.
abstract: Despite the well-established link between animal abuse and interpersonal violence, animal mistreatment remains a global issue. Challenges such as inconsistent legislation, limited training of specialized pathologists, and lack of regional data persist and must be addressed. In Spain, the real incidence of animal abuse is unknown, and the literature on the topic remains scarce. This study aims to assess the evolution of feline abuse cases in the Community of Madrid, Spain, since the publication of a previous study in the same region. Over a five-year period (2020-2024), 53 cats with suspected abuse were diagnosed at the Pathology and Forensic Veterinary Unit of the VISAVET Health Surveillance Center. Thirty-one cats (58.49%) died from non-natural causes: 17 (32.07%) due to blunt force trauma, eight (15.09%) due to poisoning, and six (11.32%) due to projectile injuries. Natural causes accounted for 21 cases (39.62%). Compared to the previous study, data suggest a possible upward trend in the number of cats referred with suspected animal abuse, including eight new cases of ethylene glycol poisoning. The correlation between the type of suspected abuse and final diagnosis was very low. This article examines current challenges related to animal violence, with particular emphasis on feline colonies, and promotes awareness among both veterinary and non-veterinary professionals.

mcqs.q: In a 5-year retrospective study (2020–2024) of 53 cats with suspected abuse at a forensic veterinary unit in Madrid, Spain, among the cats that died of non-natural causes, the leading cause of death was:
mcqs.e: Blunt force trauma accounted for 32% of the Madrid cases, exceeding poisoning (15%) and projectile injury (11%).

mcqs.q: In a 5-year forensic study of 53 suspected feline abuse cases in Madrid, Spain (2020–2024), what was the correlation between the presumed type of abuse and the confirmed forensic diagnosis?
mcqs.e: The Madrid study reported a very low correlation between presumed abuse type and confirmed forensic diagnosis, underscoring the need for objective post-mortem investigation.

mcqs.q: When the correlation between suspected abuse type and confirmed forensic diagnosis is very low (as observed in feline abuse case series), this most supports which principle for forensic investigation?
o: Field impressions reliably predict cause of death
Objective necropsy/toxicology is required to establish cause and manner
mcqs.e: A very low correlation between field impressions and confirmed findings means presumptive assessments are unreliable; objective necropsy and toxicology are essential to establish cause and manner of death.

title: Five years of veterinary forensic necropsies in the Netherlands: a retrospective analysis of non-human cases
citation: Monique Verkerk, Thomas P. Shehata. Five years of veterinary forensic necropsies in the Netherlands: a retrospective analysis of non-human cases. International Journal of Legal Medicine. 2026.
abstract: In this study a five-year retrospective analysis (2020-2024) of veterinary forensic necropsies in the Netherlands is presented, based on 346 necropsies out of 390 total submissions to Stichting Forensisch Dierenonderzoek (Forensic Animal Research Foundation), involving suspected non-natural deaths with potential forensic relevance. The objective was to characterize animal abuse cases by assessing species involvement, presumptive causes and manners of death based on gross findings, and regional, temporal, and procedural patterns. Forensic necropsies were performed according to standardized internal protocols, and data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics. The majority of examined animals were companion species, particularly dogs (41.8%) and cats (28.5%). Presumptively classified non-natural deaths accounted for 66.8% of cases, while natural deaths represented 9.5%, accidents 8.4%, and undetermined cases 15.3%. Among non-natural deaths, blunt force trauma (30.3%) and neglect or deprivation (26.4%) were the most frequent causes, based on gross necropsy findings. Seasonal variation in decomposition stage and regional disparities in submissions were observed. Submission and packaging practices improved modestly over time, yet forensic standards were not consistently met. Legal outcomes were retrieved for 80 cases: most resulted in minor penalties such as fines or community service, with only one case leading to imprisonment exceeding six months. These findings underscore the dominance of violent and neglect-related deaths in Dutch veterinary forensic caseloads and emphasize the need for standardized protocols, interdisciplinary collaboration, and institutional support for veterinary forensic science.

mcqs.e: Blunt force trauma (30.3%) and neglect/deprivation (26.4%) dominated non-natural deaths in this Dutch forensic series.

mcqs.q: In a 5-year Dutch veterinary forensic necropsy series (2020–2024, n=346), legal outcomes were retrieved for 80 cases. These outcomes were generally:
o: Minor penalties such as fines or community service
mcqs.e: Most outcomes were minor penalties such as fines or community service; only one case resulted in imprisonment exceeding six months.

mcqs.q: In a 5-year Dutch veterinary forensic necropsy study (2020–2024, n=346 necropsies), the most commonly examined companion species were:
mcqs.e: Companion species predominated: dogs (41.8%) and cats (28.5%) of all examined animals.

title: Markers of inflammation and infection are associated with prolonged recovery in dogs emaciated from long-term inadequate nutrition
authors: Sylvia M. Lesnikowski, Sharon Pailler, Emily G. Patterson-Kane
citation: Sylvia M. Lesnikowski, Sharon Pailler, Emily G. Patterson-Kane. Markers of inflammation and infection are associated with prolonged recovery in dogs emaciated from long-term inadequate nutrition. American Journal of Veterinary Research (AJVR). 2025.
abstract: Objective: To characterize the presentation of underweight dogs suffering from long-term inadequate nutrition (LTIN) in suspected cases of animal cruelty, evaluate the efficacy of a feeding protocol, and investigate factors associated with prolonged recovery. Methods: This was a retrospective review of records evaluating 246 emaciated adult dogs involved in suspected cases of animal cruelty from January 1, 2015, through December 31, 2020. Data, including history, weight, clinical signs, parasite test results, hematologic, and urinalysis results, were extracted from the records. Logistic regression models were used to identify significant predictors of delayed weight gain. Results: Most cases were pit bull-type dogs (180 of 246 [73.2%]) with a body condition score of 1/9 (145 of 246 [58.9%]). No dogs died from medical issues related to LTIN. The mean time for dogs to regain 20% body weight was 4.4 weeks, and the mean time for 30% weight gain was 6.4 weeks. In a multivariable analysis, dogs with hyperglobulinemia and neutrophilia were more likely to take more than 4 weeks to reach 20% of their intake body weight, and dogs with hyperglobulinemia and monocytosis were more likely to take more than 6 weeks to reach 30% of their intake body weight. Conclusions: This feeding protocol resulted in successful weight gain in dogs that were emaciated due to LTIN. Indicators of inflammation and/or infection were associated with a longer recovery time. Clinical relevance: Since this feeding protocol resulted in successful weight gain without adverse outcomes, it is recommended for dogs with LTIN.

mcqs.q: The structured refeeding protocol for emaciated cruelty-case dogs resulted in:
o: Safe weight gain with no nutrition-related deaths
mcqs.e: No dogs died of nutrition-related issues and the protocol produced successful weight gain.

mcqs.q: In a retrospective study of 246 emaciated adult dogs from suspected animal cruelty cases, which laboratory findings were associated with prolonged recovery (delayed weight gain)?
mcqs.e: Markers of inflammation/infection — hyperglobulinemia combined with neutrophilia (predictor of >4-week recovery) or monocytosis (predictor of >6-week recovery) — were associated with delayed weight gain in cruelty-case dogs.

mcqs.q: The forensic significance of documented weight gain on a controlled diet is that it:
o: Indicates prior weight loss was from withheld food (neglect), not disease
mcqs.e: Recovery on adequate feeding is strong evidence the emaciation resulted from food deprivation.

title: Retrospective classification of veterinary forensic cases from the archives of the Italian Istituti Zooprofilattici Sperimentali (2013-2023)
authors: Daniela Averaimo, Alessandra Scagliarini, Pietro Badagliacca, Stefania Salucci, Lucio Marino, Massimiliano Paoletti, Antonio Cocco, Elga E. Tieri, Maria Chiara Cantelmi, Sabrina V. P. Defourny, Angelo Peli, Antonio Petrini
citation: Daniela Averaimo, Alessandra Scagliarini, Pietro Badagliacca, Stefania Salucci, Lucio Marino, Massimiliano Paoletti, Antonio Cocco, Elga E. Tieri, Maria Chiara Cantelmi, Sabrina V. P. Defourny, Angelo Peli, Antonio Petrini. Retrospective classification of veterinary forensic cases from the archives of the Italian Istituti Zooprofilattici Sperimentali (2013-2023). Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 2026.
abstract: Introduction: Definitive guidelines for the classification of cases in Veterinary Forensic Medicine (VFM) are currently unavailable. An attempt to classify lesions observed in forensic necropsies was proposed in 2022 following the codes of the ICD-11. The archives of the Istituti Zooprofilattici Sperimentali (IIZZSS) are structured to identify forensic pathology cases using pre-coded information only on wild animals' mortality and suspected animal poisonings at the time of acceptance. In contrast, other forensic documentation sources, including non-pre-coded necropsy diagnoses, require interpretation based on laboratory test results and accompanying expert opinions. Methods: This study proposes the classification of previously unclassified VFM cases through a three-step approach: (1) data analysis, (2) review and classification of expert opinions by assigning labels corresponding to the main forensic topics, and (3) organization of diagnoses into categories and subcategories. Cases recorded in the database of the Istituto Zooprofilattico Sperimentale dell'Abruzzo e del Molise between 2013 and 2023 were retrospectively evaluated. Results: A total of 1,221 non-coded cases with an expert opinion were identified. Among these, 405 cases (33.16%) were classified as potential Veterinary Forensic Cases and categorized into five macro-categories and 19 subcategories. The main cause of mortality differed according to animal type: injury was the most frequent cause in pets, attack in livestock, and unlawful killing in wildlife. Discussion: This classification approach enabled the identification and organization of previously unclassified VFM cases within the institutional database. Poisoning cases and wild animal deaths caused by vehicular collisions were excluded as they were already pre-classified. Therefore, the reported percentages refer only to this subset of cases and do not reflect the overall mortality rates in the region.

mcqs.q: In a retrospective classification of veterinary forensic cases from the Italian Istituti Zooprofilattici Sperimentali archives (2013–2023), the leading forensic cause of death in pets was:
mcqs.e: Injury was the most frequent cause in pets, in contrast to attack in livestock and unlawful killing in wildlife.

mcqs.q: In a retrospective review of veterinary forensic cases from Italian national animal health institute (Istituti Zooprofilattici Sperimentali) archives (2013–2023), the leading forensic cause of death among wildlife was:
mcqs.e: Unlawful killing was the dominant cause among wildlife, versus injury in pets and attack in livestock.

mcqs.q: An Italian retrospective study proposing a classification framework for veterinary forensic medicine (VFM) cases from archives spanning 2013–2023 highlights which critical gap in the field?
o: Absence of standardized forensic case-classification (e.g., ICD-11-style coding)
mcqs.e: Definitive classification guidelines for veterinary forensic medicine are currently unavailable; the study proposes an ICD-11-style coding approach to identify and organize previously unclassified cases in institutional archives.

title: Ethylene glycol poisoning in a free-roaming cat associated with suspected animal cruelty: a forensic veterinary case report in South Korea
authors: A. Y. Kim, M. Kang, H. Choi, M. Park, J. S. Baek, B. Ku, K. Lee
citation: A. Y. Kim, M. Kang, H. Choi, M. Park, J. S. Baek, B. Ku, K. Lee. Ethylene glycol poisoning in a free-roaming cat associated with suspected animal cruelty: a forensic veterinary case report in South Korea. Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 2026.
abstract: Ethylene glycol (EG) is a common cause of fatal poisoning in companion animals and may be involved in intentional or negligent animal cruelty. We describe a forensic veterinary investigation of a free-roaming cat submitted by the Seoul Gangbuk Police in relation to an alleged violation of the Korean Animal Protection Act. Complete necropsy revealed focal gastric erosion and bilaterally congested kidneys, while histopathology of the kidneys showed acute tubular epithelial necrosis with abundant intraluminal calcium oxalate crystal deposition. Toxicological analysis of gastric tissue using a validated GC-MS method demonstrated the presence of ethylene glycol and its primary metabolite glycolic acid, confirming ethylene glycol exposure and, together with the gross and microscopic renal lesions, supporting antifreeze poisoning as the cause of death. PCR testing of pooled tissue samples was positive for feline parvovirus and feces were positive for feline coronavirus, but these infections were not considered the proximate cause of death. This case highlights the value of forensic veterinary pathology and toxicology in objectively determining cause of death in suspected animal cruelty investigations and demonstrates that targeted analysis of gastric tissue can provide definitive evidence of ethylene glycol exposure.

mcqs.q: The classic histopathologic hallmark of ethylene glycol (antifreeze) toxicosis in the kidneys is:
o: Renal tubular necrosis with calcium oxalate crystals
mcqs.e: Acute tubular epithelial necrosis with abundant intraluminal calcium oxalate crystal deposition is the pathognomonic renal finding of ethylene glycol toxicosis.

mcqs.q: In a South Korean forensic veterinary case report of a free-roaming cat that died of ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning, concurrent PCR-positive results for feline parvovirus and feline coronavirus were interpreted as:
o: Not the proximate cause of death
The cause of the renal lesions
mcqs.e: These viral infections were present but were not considered the proximate cause of death; the renal lesions and toxicological findings were consistent with antifreeze poisoning.

mcqs.q: In a forensic veterinary investigation of ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning in a cat, definitive confirmation of exposure was achieved by analyzing gastric tissue using:
o: Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) detection of ethylene glycol and glycolic acid
mcqs.e: A validated GC-MS method detected both ethylene glycol and its primary metabolite glycolic acid in gastric tissue, confirming antifreeze exposure.

title: A Retrospective Study of Suspected Animal Abuse Cases in Trinidad and Tobago, 2008-2025
authors: Karelma Frontera-Acevedo, Alanis Boodram, Xaria Luke, Emily Phillip, Rod Suepaul, Lana Gyan
citation: Karelma Frontera-Acevedo, Alanis Boodram, Xaria Luke, Emily Phillip, Rod Suepaul, Lana Gyan. A Retrospective Study of Suspected Animal Abuse Cases in Trinidad and Tobago, 2008-2025. Animals (MDPI). 2026.
abstract: Forensic veterinary pathology is becoming increasingly important in investigating situations of suspected animal abuse. In Trinidad and Tobago, there are only two veterinary diagnostic laboratories capable of performing necropsies, one at the University of the West Indies School of Veterinary Medicine (UWI-SVM) and the other at the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory (MAF-VDL). The databases of both UWI-SVM and MAF-VDL were searched for cases of suspected animal abuse between 2008 and 2025. Based on pathology records and case submission information, cases were categorized by year, species, cause of death (COD) or manner of injury (MOI), police submissions, and types of trauma and poisonings. A total of 113 cases of suspected animal abuse were submitted in the years 2008-2025. Case submissions reached a peak in 2015 (n = 23). The most submitted animal species was dogs (77%). Of the 113 cases, only 24 (20%) had a confirmed COD/MOI. The most common confirmed COD/MOI was trauma. The few confirmed cases of poisoning (n = 6) include carbamates, warfarin, malathion, and ethylene glycol. Owners appear to be aware of the importance of pathology to help diagnose suspected animal abuse cases. One major limitation in advancing forensic veterinary pathology on the island, and a factor preventing the prosecution of suspected animal abuse cases, is the lack of a toxicological laboratory capable of handling animal samples.

mcqs.q: In a retrospective study of 113 suspected animal abuse cases submitted to veterinary diagnostic laboratories in Trinidad and Tobago (2008–2025), approximately what proportion had a confirmed cause of death or manner of injury?
mcqs.e: Only 24 of 113 cases (20%) had a confirmed cause of death or manner of injury; trauma was the most common confirmed finding.

mcqs.q: In a retrospective review of 113 suspected animal abuse submissions to veterinary diagnostic laboratories in Trinidad and Tobago (2008–2025), the most frequently submitted species was:
mcqs.e: Dogs accounted for 77% of case submissions in this Caribbean forensic series.

mcqs.q: In Trinidad and Tobago, the main institutional barrier to confirming animal poisoning and enabling prosecution of suspected animal abuse cases was:
o: Lack of an animal toxicology laboratory
mcqs.e: Absence of a toxicological laboratory capable of handling animal samples prevented confirmation of poisoning cases and limited prosecutions.

title: Characteristics of Three Forensic Veterinary Cases Involving Pet Deaths in Domestic Murder-Suicide Incidents
authors: Yuko Kihara, Yohsuke Makino, Suguru Torimitsu, Fumiko Chiba, Hirotaro Iwase, Makoto Nakajima, Aki Tanaka
citation: Yuko Kihara, Yohsuke Makino, Suguru Torimitsu, Fumiko Chiba, Hirotaro Iwase, Makoto Nakajima, Aki Tanaka. Characteristics of Three Forensic Veterinary Cases Involving Pet Deaths in Domestic Murder-Suicide Incidents. Animals (MDPI). 2025.
abstract: Murder-suicide, also referred to as homicide-suicide, results in multiple casualties. The victims are typically human, and cases involving the inclusion of pets, sometimes termed 'murder-suicide-peticide', have been rarely reported worldwide. The aim of this study is to present and examine the characteristics of three forensic veterinary cases in which pets were found dead alongside human victims in suspected domestic murder-suicide incidents in Japan. We analyzed information provided by the police agency about the owners, families, and the animals, as well as necropsy findings of three cases. In all three cases, it was determined that both the human and animal victims died from the same cause, suggesting a tendency for perpetrators to kill pets using the same methods as those used on human victims. Murder-suicide is regarded as the most extreme form of domestic violence and abuse. Ongoing interdisciplinary research is essential for developing effective intervention strategies to protect vulnerable individuals, both human and non-human, within the household.

mcqs.q: In a Japanese forensic veterinary case series of three domestic murder-suicide incidents in which pets were found dead alongside human victims, the animals died:
o: By the same cause/mechanism as the human victims
mcqs.e: In all three cases, human and animal victims died from the same cause, suggesting perpetrators used identical lethal methods on both.

mcqs.q: Forensic reports of pets killed by the same mechanism as human victims in domestic murder-suicide incidents ('murder-suicide-peticide') provide concrete evidence supporting:
o: The Link between animal cruelty and interpersonal/family violence
mcqs.e: Pet co-victimization in extreme domestic violence reinforces The Link — the well-established connection between animal cruelty and interpersonal violence.

mcqs.q: Given that pets are sometimes killed alongside human victims in domestic murder-suicide incidents, forensic veterinary researchers most strongly support which practical intervention:
o: Cross-reporting between human and animal welfare agencies
mcqs.e: Interdisciplinary collaboration and cross-reporting between human and animal welfare agencies are recommended to protect all vulnerable household members.

title: Case report - Animal abuse by condition falsification in a dog with epileptic seizures caused by citalopram poisoning
authors: Ineke R. van Herwijnen, Daphne G. L. van Helvoort, Anton H. A. Beijer
citation: Ineke R. van Herwijnen, Daphne G. L. van Helvoort, Anton H. A. Beijer. Case report - Animal abuse by condition falsification in a dog with epileptic seizures caused by citalopram poisoning. Forensic Science International. 2026.
abstract: Animal abuse by condition falsification so far has received little scientific attention. This particular form of animal abuse is characterized by an animal caretaker's infliction of harm to an animal by feigning a condition with the purpose to get attention or sympathy from others, such as veterinary personnel. We report the case of a young dog with early onset and recurrent epileptic seizures in which post-mortem examination revealed citalopram poisoning. Red flags were in the early onset of the seizures in this dog in combination with previous dogs from the household also suffering epileptic seizures. This case report highlights the importance of considering animal abuse by condition falsification and the relevance of toxicological testing in suspected cases, as to prevent animal suffering and untimely death.

mcqs.q: Animal abuse by condition falsification is the veterinary analog of:
o: Munchausen syndrome by proxy (factitious disorder by proxy)
mcqs.e: The caretaker feigns/induces a condition to gain attention or sympathy—analogous to factitious disorder by proxy.

mcqs.q: In a published case report of animal abuse by condition falsification involving a young dog with recurrent epileptic seizures, post-mortem toxicological examination revealed the seizures were caused by:
mcqs.e: Post-mortem examination confirmed citalopram (an antidepressant) poisoning — deliberately administered by the caretaker to simulate epilepsy.

mcqs.q: In a case of animal abuse by condition falsification (deliberate inducement of seizures to gain veterinary attention), the clinical red flags that prompted suspicion of factitious harm were:
o: Early onset plus a household history of prior dogs with seizures
mcqs.e: Atypically early-onset seizures in the current dog, combined with previous household dogs also having seizures, were warning signs of deliberate harm rather than idiopathic epilepsy.

title: Overkilling in a Dog: A Case Report
authors: Fabio Pesce, E. Sannino, E. Ragosta, L. Marigliano, G. Picazio, M. Esposito, M. Dimatteo, B. Degli Uberti, S. De Luca, N. Di Caprio, D. Citarella, R. Pinto, G. Fusco, E. De Carlo, G. Miletti
citation: Fabio Pesce, E. Sannino, E. Ragosta, L. Marigliano, G. Picazio, M. Esposito, M. Dimatteo, B. Degli Uberti, S. De Luca, N. Di Caprio, D. Citarella, R. Pinto, G. Fusco, E. De Carlo, G. Miletti. Overkilling in a Dog: A Case Report. Animals (MDPI). 2025.
abstract: The term 'overkilling' in forensic medicine is not clearly defined and is used to refer to homicides involving unusually massive injuries, far exceeding those necessary to kill the victim. This is the clinical case of a dog found in February 2023 in a town near Naples, with a rope around its neck and the metacarpal region of its forelimbs. The dog was taken to the Istituto Zooprofilattico Sperimentale del Mezzogiorno (IZSM, Portici, Southern Italy), where it underwent a total body radiographic study performed using the 'Philosophy HF400' X-ray device (Pan Vet, Kildare Town, Ireland). Subsequently, a full autopsy was performed, and samples of the injured organs were analyzed by accredited in-house laboratories for microbiological, histological and toxicological analyses. The autopsy revealed anatomopathological lesions compatible with strangulation, which were confirmed by histological examination. The autopsy also reported serosanguineous chest effusion, food material mixed with blackish microgranules and harmful substances in the stomach and, finally, uncoagulated blood in the atrioventricular chambers of the heart. These findings raised the suspicion of poisoning, which was confirmed by the positive outcome of toxicological tests.

mcqs.q: In forensic medicine, 'overkilling' refers to:
o: Injury far exceeding what is necessary to cause death
mcqs.e: Overkilling denotes unusually massive injuries beyond those needed to kill the victim.

mcqs.q: In a forensic veterinary case report of an 'overkilling' incident involving a dog found with rope restraints in southern Italy, the two concurrent lethal mechanisms confirmed at autopsy were:
mcqs.e: Strangulation lesions were confirmed histologically, and toxicological testing confirmed concurrent poisoning — demonstrating lethal force far exceeding what was necessary to cause death.

mcqs.q: In a forensic veterinary overkilling case involving both strangulation and poisoning in a dog, the workup that revealed both concurrent lethal mechanisms comprised:
o: Combined radiography, autopsy, histology, and toxicology
mcqs.e: Full-body radiography, gross autopsy, histopathology, and toxicology together exposed the dual lethal mechanisms in this overkilling case.

title: Advances in Forensic Toxicology in Veterinary Medicine: Current Perspectives, Analytical Progress, and Future Challenges
authors: Giulio Mannocchi, Filippo Roberto Busardò, Luigi Tonino Marsella, Roberta Tittarelli
citation: Giulio Mannocchi, Filippo Roberto Busardò, Luigi Tonino Marsella, Roberta Tittarelli. Advances in Forensic Toxicology in Veterinary Medicine: Current Perspectives, Analytical Progress, and Future Challenges. Veterinary Sciences (MDPI). 2026.
abstract: Over the past decade, veterinary forensic toxicology has gained increasing relevance due to the recognition of animal poisoning as a criminal, environmental, and public health concern. This review provides an updated overview on current perspectives in veterinary forensic toxicology, focusing on common toxicological scenarios, analytical innovations, and interpretative challenges. Intentional poisoning of companion animals, wildlife intoxication, and environmental contamination are discussed within a One Health framework. Mass spectrometry-based techniques, including targeted gas chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (GC-MS/MS), liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) for non-targeted screening, and emerging ambient mass spectrometry approaches are highlighted as pivotal tools in modern forensic investigations. Major limitations related to post-mortem changes, species-specific toxicokinetic, and the lack of harmonized interpretative criteria are critically examined. The review also identified future priorities such as methodological standardization, expansion of toxicokinetic databases across species, detection of emerging contaminants, and strengthened international cooperation. Overall, veterinary forensic toxicology is an emerging discipline at the intersection of animal welfare, environmental conservation, and public health providing essential evidence for legal, regulatory, and investigative purposes.

mcqs.q: A 2026 review of advances in veterinary forensic toxicology identifies which major interpretive limitations as complicating the discipline?
o: Post-mortem changes, species-specific toxicokinetics, and lack of harmonized interpretative criteria
An overabundance of standardized interpretative criteria
Excessive toxicokinetic databases across all species
A complete absence of analytical instrumentation
mcqs.e: The review critically examines post-mortem changes, species-specific toxicokinetics, and the lack of harmonized interpretative criteria as major limitations in veterinary forensic toxicology.

mcqs.q: In veterinary forensic toxicology, which analytical platform is highlighted as the mainstay for detecting and confirming toxic substances?
o: Mass spectrometry-based techniques (gas chromatography–tandem MS [GC-MS/MS], liquid chromatography–tandem MS [LC-MS/MS], high-resolution MS [HRMS])
mcqs.e: Mass spectrometry-based techniques — including GC-MS/MS, LC-MS/MS, and HRMS for non-targeted screening — are emphasized as pivotal forensic tools for targeted and untargeted detection.

mcqs.q: According to a 2026 review on advances in veterinary forensic toxicology, intentional animal poisoning is best framed as:
o: Both a cruelty crime and a public/environmental health hazard (One Health)
mcqs.e: The review situates animal poisoning at the intersection of animal welfare, environmental conservation, and public health — a One Health concern, not merely an isolated cruelty crime.

title: A Practical Diagnostic Approach to Non-Drowning Asphyxia in Animals: Forensic Pathology and Biomarkers
authors: Veronica Romano, Davide De Biase, Valeria Russo, Evaristo Di Napoli, Orlando Paciello, Giuseppe Piegari
citation: Veronica Romano, Davide De Biase, Valeria Russo, Evaristo Di Napoli, Orlando Paciello, Giuseppe Piegari. A Practical Diagnostic Approach to Non-Drowning Asphyxia in Animals: Forensic Pathology and Biomarkers. Veterinary Sciences (MDPI). 2026.
abstract: The term asphyxia refers to a disruption in brain function due to rapid and persistent cerebral hypoxia or anoxia as a consequence of accidental or non-accidental injury. Considering the different mechanisms that may determine asphyxiation, such injuries can be referred to different categories: strangulation (death by hanging, ligature or manual strangulation), suffocation (smothering, choking, confined spaces and vitiated atmosphere), mechanical asphyxia (positional and traumatic asphyxia) and drowning (submersion or immersion in liquid). In both human and veterinary forensic practice, fatal asphyxia is considered among the most diagnostically challenging categories of sudden death, as it often produces only subtle and non-pathognomonic macroscopic signs, which can be easily covered by post-mortem alterations. Therefore, a wide range of information is often needed for the diagnosis of asphyxiation, including medical history, crime scene analysis, testimonies and physical evidence, along with the macroscopic and histological findings. The following review addresses the main lesions, ancillary tests and diagnostic issues associated with non-drowning asphyxia in veterinary forensic pathology.

mcqs.q: Why is fatal non-drowning asphyxia one of the hardest forensic diagnoses to confirm at necropsy?
o: It produces florid pathognomonic lesions that confuse examiners
Gross findings are subtle, non-specific, and easily masked by postmortem change
It always requires toxicology that is rarely available
Asphyxial deaths leave no histological changes at all
mcqs.e: The review stresses asphyxia yields only subtle, non-pathognomonic gross signs readily obscured by postmortem alterations.

mcqs.q: In veterinary forensic pathology, which of the following is NOT one of the recognized categories of asphyxia-related death?
mcqs.e: The recognized forensic asphyxia categories are strangulation, suffocation, mechanical asphyxia, and drowning. Anaphylactic asphyxia is not among them.

mcqs.q: What does reliable diagnosis of asphyxiation depend on?
o: Integrating scene context, history, and ancillary histology/biomarkers rather than gross necropsy alone
Excluding all other causes by toxicology only
mcqs.e: Because gross signs are non-specific, diagnosis requires synthesizing history, scene analysis, and ancillary tests.

title: Veterinarians' perspectives on animal welfare, legal enforcement, and forensic readiness in companion animal cruelty investigations in Thailand: A cross-sectional qualitative study
authors: Apichaya Lorsirigool, Yutthana Sudjaroen, Nuttapon Kulnides, Natapol Pumipuntu, Atthaporn Roongsitthichai, Supawadee Piratae, Maluna Intrakamhaeng, Sirintip Chaiyasak, Kanokwan Saenkaew
citation: Apichaya Lorsirigool, Yutthana Sudjaroen, Nuttapon Kulnides, Natapol Pumipuntu, Atthaporn Roongsitthichai, Supawadee Piratae, Maluna Intrakamhaeng, Sirintip Chaiyasak, Kanokwan Saenkaew. Veterinarians' perspectives on animal welfare, legal enforcement, and forensic readiness in companion animal cruelty investigations in Thailand: A cross-sectional qualitative study. Veterinary World. 2026.
abstract: Animal cruelty is a persistent concern for animal welfare and society worldwide. In Thailand, the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals and Animal Welfare Act B.E. 2557 (2014) provides a legal framework to address animal abuse; however, effective enforcement remains constrained by limitations in investigative procedures and the limited integration of veterinary forensic science. Veterinarians from the Department of Livestock Development (DLD) play a central role in responding to cruelty reports, conducting inspections, and supporting legal processes. This study aimed to explore the attitudes of DLD veterinarians toward companion animal welfare, the effectiveness of existing animal welfare legislation, and the current and potential role of forensic science in animal cruelty investigations in Thailand. A cross-sectional qualitative study was conducted between August 2024 and December 2024. Eighteen veterinarians with DLD from six geographic regions of Thailand were recruited using stratified purposive sampling. Data were collected via a validated, open-ended online questionnaire that addressed animal welfare challenges, legal enforcement, investigative procedures, and forensic applications. Qualitative content analysis was performed using the NVivo software, with double-blind coding to enhance analytical rigor. Multiple interrelated drivers of companion animal cruelty were identified by veterinarians. The major welfare-related themes included a lack of owner responsibility and preparedness, insufficient knowledge and ethical awareness regarding animal care, socioeconomic constraints, deficiencies in stray animal management systems, weaknesses in law enforcement, and cultural attitudes that undermine animal welfare. While most respondents perceived the existing animal cruelty law as partially effective in reducing abuse, they highlighted critical gaps, including ambiguous legal definitions, inconsistent enforcement, and limited public awareness.
